rookie_w1_l1.title: Letters A to M
rookie_w1_l1.summary: Say each letter name out loud, then its sound.
rookie_w1_l1.subject: reading

content.explain: These are the first half of the alphabet: A, B, C, all the way to M. Say each letter name out loud, then make its sound with me!
examples:
Grown-up says the letter, Rookie points: A, B, C, D.
Then swap: Rookie says it and the grown-up points.

Sound game: the grown-up says 'ah' and Rookie finds the letter A.
Keep it bouncy: three letters, then a giggle.

practice.question: Which letter comes right after F?
practice.hint: Say A B C D E F ... and listen for the next one.
practice.praise: Yes! G comes after F.

practice.question: Which of these is the FIRST letter of the alphabet?
practice.hint: It is the very first letter we sing.
practice.praise: Yay! A is first.

practice.question: Which letter says sss?
practice.hint: It is the sound a snake makes.
practice.praise: Yes! S says sss.

practice.question: Which letter sits between B and D?
practice.hint: Say B, ..., D out loud and catch the middle letter.
practice.praise: Great! C is in the middle.

practice.praise: Great! Y is in the middle.

rookie_w2_l1.summary: Count together out loud, nice and slow.
rookie_w2_l1.subject: math

content.explain: We count up to 10 on our fingers, one number for each finger. Say the numbers slow and steady while you point at each toy as you go.
examples:
Grown-up holds up fingers one by one. Count together: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5!
Now count the other hand: 6, 7, 8, 9, 10. Yay!
Count the snacks on the plate together, touching each one as you say the number.

practice.question: Count with me: 1, 2, 3, ___
practice.hint: One more than 3.
practice.praise: Right! 4 comes next.

practice.question: How many fingers are on ONE hand?
practice.hint: Hold up one hand and count them.
practice.praise: Yay! One hand has 5 fingers.

practice.question: Which number is bigger?
practice.hint: Count up: 2 ... 7.
practice.praise: Great! 7 is bigger than 2.

Then 16, 17, 18, 19, 20 ... big clap!
Point at the blocks while counting: one touch, one number.

practice.praise: Yay! 19 comes after 18.

practice.question: Count with me: 11, 12, ___

practice.praise: Great! 13 comes next.

rookie_w2_l3.title: More or Less
rookie_w2_l3.summary: Which group has more? Tap the bigger one.
rookie_w2_l3.subject: math

content.explain: More means the bigger group and less means the smaller one. Count both groups, then tap the one with more.
examples:
Grown-up makes two groups of blocks: 3 and 5.
Count each: 3 ... 5. The group of 5 has more!
Now swap: 2 and 4. Which has more? Rookie counts, then taps.

practice.praise: Yes! 5 apples is more.

practice.question: Which number is more, 8 or 6?

practice.praise: Right! 8 is more than 6.

practice.question: Which number is less, 2 or 9?
practice.hint: Less means the smaller group.
practice.praise: Yay! 2 is the smaller one.

Now add one more car: what is the new count? (7)
Sort the toys into two piles first, then count each pile.

practice.praise: Yes! 4 and 1 more makes 5.

practice.question: How many teddies do you count?

practice.praise: Right! There are 5 teddies.

practice.question: Which group has more?
practice.hint: Count each group first.
practice.praise: Yay! 4 cars is more.

juniper_w1_l1.title: Skip-Counting Patterns
juniper_w1_l1.summary: Count by 2s, 5s, and 10s to see how multiplication grows.
juniper_w1_l1.subject: math

content.explain: Skip-counting means you add the same number every time instead of counting by ones. Counting by 5s goes 5, 10, 15, 20. It is the fast path to multiplication, because every jump is one more group. Count out loud while you tap your fingers.
examples:
Count by 2s:
2, 4, 6, 8, 10
Every jump adds 2 more than the last number.

Count by 5s:
5, 10, 15, 20, 25
Each jump lands on a new handful of fingers.

Count by 10s:
10, 20, 30, 40
Four jumps of 10 gets you to 40.

practice.question: What number comes next?  5, 10, 15, ___
practice.hint: Add 5 to the last number you said.

practice.question: Which list counts by 2s?
practice.hint: Each number should be 2 more than the one before it.
practice.praise: Right! Every number jumps by 2.

practice.question: Which list counts by 10s?
practice.hint: Look for jumps of exactly 10.
practice.praise: Nice! 10, 20, 30, 40 jumps by 10 each time.

practice.question: If you count by 3s, what is the 4th number?  3, 6, 9, ___
practice.hint: Add 3 to the last number.
practice.praise: Exactly! 9 + 3 = 12.

workbook.prompt: Write the next five numbers in a count-by-3s pattern from 3.
workbook.answer: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18 - each jump adds 3.

workbook.prompt: Circle every number in a skip count that lands on a multiple of 10.
workbook.answer: Every 10s number in the pattern is circled.

workbook.prompt: Write a count-by-2s pattern that reaches 20 and one that reaches 30.
Explain in one sentence why skip counting helps with multiplication.
workbook.answer: Because each jump is one more group of the same size.

juniper_w1_rd1.title: Read It and Mark New Words
juniper_w1_rd1.summary: First read for the story, second read for the words you do not know.
juniper_w1_rd1.subject: reading

content.explain: Read the passage twice. The first time is only for the story, so enjoy it and keep your finger moving. The second time, slow down and underline THREE words you do not know. Do not stop at the word itself: read the whole sentence around it, because the sentence usually tells you what the word means. Write your best guess in the margin, then check it with a grown-up or a dictionary.

examples.q:
Passage line: Maya asked the librarian if anyone had returned it.
Unknown word: librarian
The sentence tells you she works at the library.
examples.a: librarian = the person who works at the library and helps you find books.
steps: Find the clue near the word.
Write your guess, then check it.

examples.q:
You read: One Tuesday the big book was missing from the shelf.
What does missing mean here?
examples.a: Gone, not where it should be.
steps: Ask what happened to the book.
Say the meaning in your own words.

examples.q: Underline three hard words in one paragraph.
examples.a: Example set: librarian, return bin, reading room.
steps: Guess each meaning from its sentence.

workbook.prompt: Underline three words you do not know in today's passage.
workbook.answer: Three clear underlines, one per new word, in the reading block.

workbook.prompt: Pick one underlined word and write what you THINK it means.
workbook.answer: A guess written in the margin in your own words - for example: librarian = works at the library.

workbook.prompt: Read the sentence around that word again and write a better meaning.
workbook.answer: A second, clearer meaning that uses the clue in the sentence.

workbook.prompt: Tell your grown-up what happened FIRST in the story, then what happened next.
workbook.answer: A two-part retell: first the big book was missing, then the librarian found it under the newspapers.

juniper_w1_sp1.title: Closed Syllables: The Ten Words
juniper_w1_sp1.summary: One short vowel, one closed syllable - sort the list by the rule.
juniper_w1_sp1.subject: spelling

content.explain: A closed syllable ends in a consonant and has ONE short vowel sound. That closing consonant is what keeps the vowel short: cat, bed, sit, hot, mud. When you meet a new word, clap it into syllables and ask whether each syllable is closed. If it is, the vowel says its short sound, and you already know how to spell it. This week's ten words all follow that rule, which is why sorting them by vowel sound works.

examples.q:
cat, chick, plan
All closed: each syllable ends in a consonant after one vowel.
examples.a: Short a, short i, short a again.

examples.q: Which word is a closed syllable?  table / cat / going
examples.a: table is open (ends in a vowel sound), cat is closed, going ends in a vowel sound.
steps: Check the last sound of the syllable.

examples.q: Sort: bed, drop, swim, hot by vowel sound.
examples.a: short e: bed | short o: drop, hot | short i: swim.

workbook.prompt: Write the ten spelling words in two columns: closed / not closed.
workbook.answer: All ten words in the closed column - they all end in a consonant after one vowel.

workbook.prompt: Sort the ten words by short vowel sound.
workbook.answer: Groups such as short a: cat, plan, blast; short e: bed; short i: sit, swim, chick; short o: hot, drop; short u: mud.

workbook.prompt: Circle the vowel in each of the ten words.
workbook.answer: One vowel circled per word - the single short vowel of the closed syllable.

workbook.prompt: Cover the list and write five words from memory, then check.
workbook.answer: Five words written from memory, with any misses fixed in a new colour.

juniper_w1_sci1.title: Living and Non-Living Things
juniper_w1_sci1.summary: Learn the lesson, then tell a parent three facts without looking.
juniper_w1_sci1.subject: science

content.explain: Living things share four jobs: they grow, they need food and water, they move on their own, and they respond to the world around them. Non-living things do none of those jobs - a rock never grows and a spoon never eats. Some things WERE living, like a fallen leaf or a shell, and now they are not. Scientists sort the world by evidence, so look for the job a thing does before you decide which group it belongs to.

examples.q: A dog: grows, eats, breathes, moves by itself.
examples.a: Living.

examples.q: A rock: never grows, never eats, never breathes.
examples.a: Not living.

examples.q: A dead leaf: was living, has stopped growing.
examples.a: Once living, now not living.

workbook.prompt: Name three living things you can see from the window.
workbook.answer: Three real living things, each with one job it does (grows, eats, moves).

workbook.prompt: Name three non-living things in this room.
workbook.answer: Three non-living things, each with a reason it is not alive.

workbook.prompt: Explain why a mushroom IS living.
workbook.answer: Because it grows and needs food - not because it looks like a plant.

workbook.prompt: Explain why a cloud is NOT living.
workbook.answer: Because it never eats, grows or breathes - it is weather, not life.

juniper_w1_hist1.title: Community Helpers in Order
juniper_w1_hist1.summary: Read the lesson and put four events or people in the right order.
juniper_w1_hist1.subject: history

content.explain: History is an ORDER of events, not a pile of facts. When four helpers or four events belong to a story, ask what had to happen before what. Read the timeline strip from left to right and place the first event at the start. A good check is to read your order aloud as a sentence: if it tells a sensible story, the order is probably right.

examples.q: Someone falls, you tell an adult, an adult calls the paramedics, a paramedic arrives.
examples.a: That is the correct order.
steps: Read it aloud as a story.

examples.q: Which comes first: the guard raises the sign, or the children cross?
examples.a: The guard raises the sign - children cannot cross safely first.
steps: Ask which one allows the other.

examples.q: Order: alarm rings, get dressed, bus arrives, class begins.
examples.a: A school morning in order.

workbook.prompt: Put four community-helper events in order on your timeline strip.
workbook.answer: Four events placed earliest to latest.

workbook.prompt: Read your order back as one story sentence.
workbook.answer: A sentence that makes sense when read start to finish.

workbook.prompt: Swap two cards and say why the new order is WRONG.
workbook.answer: A reason naming which step now happens before it should.

workbook.prompt: Add one helper to the timeline and place them correctly.
workbook.answer: A fifth helper inserted in a defensible position with a reason.

juniper_w1_cod1.title: Build a Sprite That Moves
juniper_w1_cod1.summary: Drag out five blocks and run the sprite - then predict before you press run.
juniper_w1_cod1.subject: coding

content.explain: An algorithm is a list of steps small enough for anyone to follow. Today you drag out FIVE blocks to make a sprite move five steps. Before you press run, read the blocks from the top and PREDICT what will happen. Prediction is the coder's habit: if the screen surprises you, go back and read the blocks again instead of guessing.

examples.q:
Blocks: say hello, move 5 steps, wait 2 seconds.
Predict: it talks, then moves, then waits.
examples.a: Top to bottom, in order.

examples.q: You predict the sprite moves 15 steps, but it moves 5.
examples.a: Re-read the blocks: how many move blocks are there really?

examples.q: Five blocks: say, move, wait, move, say.
examples.a: Order matters: swap two and the story changes.

workbook.prompt: Drag out five blocks that make your sprite move five steps.
workbook.answer: A five-block stack that runs without errors.

workbook.prompt: Write down your prediction of what will happen BEFORE you press run.
workbook.answer: A written prediction: what the sprite will say and how far it will go.

workbook.prompt: Run it and compare with your prediction.
workbook.answer: An honest match or mismatch noted beside the prediction.

workbook.prompt: Read the five blocks back in order to your grown-up.
workbook.answer: Five blocks named aloud, top to bottom.

juniper_w1_l2.title: Multiplication Facts 2-5
juniper_w1_l2.summary: Build fast recall for the 2, 3, 4, and 5 times tables.
juniper_w1_l2.subject: math

content.explain: Multiplication is adding the same number over and over. Four groups of three is 3 + 3 + 3 + 3, which is 4 x 3 = 12. Say the fact out loud twice when you learn it. Fast facts make every other math job easier.
examples:
4 x 6:
Four groups of 6.
6, 12, 18, 24.
So 4 x 6 = 24.

3 x 7:
Three groups of 7.
7, 14, 21.
So 3 x 7 = 21.

practice.question: 4 x 6 = ?
practice.hint: Count by 4s six times: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24.

practice.question: 5 x 8 = ?
practice.hint: Count by 5s eight times.
practice.praise: Great! 5 x 8 = 40.

practice.question: Which addition shows 3 x 5?
practice.hint: 3 x 5 means three groups of 5.
practice.praise: Correct! 3 x 5 is 5 + 5 + 5.

practice.question: 2 x 9 = ?
practice.hint: Two groups of 9 is 9 + 9.

workbook.prompt: Write the facts for 2 from memory.
workbook.answer: 2 x 0 through 2 x 10, written out.

workbook.prompt: Write the facts for 5 from memory.
workbook.answer: 5 x 0 through 5 x 10, written out.

workbook.prompt: Draw four groups of three and write the multiplication fact.
workbook.answer: 4 x 3 = 12, with the picture to match.

workbook.prompt: Circle the two facts you find hardest and write each twice.
workbook.answer: Two hard facts, each written twice.

juniper_w1_rd2.title: Who, What and Where
juniper_w1_rd2.summary: Answer five questions and point to the line that proves each answer.
juniper_w1_rd2.subject: reading

content.explain: A comprehension question has an answer hiding inside the text. Your job is to find the line that proves it, not to guess from memory. Ask the six question words - who, what, when, where, why and how - and hunt for the sentence that answers. When you have it, point at that line with your finger and read it aloud before you write the answer.

examples.q:
Q: Where did Maya look for the book?
Hunt: The librarian checked the return bin.
Proof line found.
examples.a: In the return bin, under a stack of newspapers.
steps: Scan for a place in the passage.
Point at the line and read it.

examples.q:
Q: Who did the book belong to?
Hunt: A name tag inside the cover said it belonged to Ben.
examples.a: Ben, a second grader.
steps: Read the whole sentence around it.

examples.q:
Q: What did Maya do next?
Hunt: she gave it back to him and chose a different story.
examples.a: She gave the book back to Ben and chose another story.

workbook.prompt: Write the answer to: Who is the passage about?
workbook.answer: The person named in the first paragraph, with the line that proves it.

workbook.prompt: Write the answer to: Where does the story happen?
workbook.answer: The place named in the passage, and you must point to that line.

workbook.prompt: Write the answer to: What was missing?
workbook.answer: The big book, proved by the sentence that says it was missing from the shelf.

workbook.prompt: Underline the exact line that proves ONE of your answers.
workbook.answer: One clean underline on a line you actually read aloud.

juniper_w1_grm1.title: Capital Letters and End Marks
juniper_w1_grm1.summary: Write four spelling words in sentences, capital first word, correct end mark.
juniper_w1_grm1.subject: english_grammar

content.explain: A sentence is a complete thought with two non-negotiable edges: a CAPITAL letter at the start and an end mark at the finish. The capital tells a reader where to begin; the period, question mark or exclamation point tells them where to stop. Today you write four spelling words inside four sentences. Before you move on, run your finger along the front of each sentence and the back of each sentence - both edges must be right.

examples.q: can we go now  ->  Can we go now?
examples.a: Capital first word, question mark last.

examples.q: i like plan  ->  I like plan.
examples.a: Capital I, period at the end.

examples.q: where is my coat  ->  Where is my coat?
examples.a: It asks, so it ends with ?

workbook.prompt: Write four spelling words, each in its own sentence.
workbook.answer: Four sentences, each containing one spelling word from the week's list.

workbook.prompt: Check every first word has a capital letter.
workbook.answer: Four capitals, one at the start of each sentence.

workbook.prompt: Check every sentence has the right end mark.
workbook.answer: Periods, question marks or exclamation points chosen to match each sentence.

workbook.prompt: Rewrite any sentence that failed either check.
workbook.answer: Corrected rewrites, not erasures.

juniper_w1_sci2.title: Checking the Six Practice Questions
juniper_w1_sci2.summary: Answer six questions on living and non-living, then check each against the lesson.
juniper_w1_sci2.subject: science

content.explain: Work the six practice questions the way a scientist works: answer first, then check. Your answer should be defensible by pointing at a line in the lesson - grows, needs food, moves, responds. If your check disagrees with your answer, do not just change the letter. Read the line, work out WHY the lesson says that, and then write the corrected answer.

examples.q:
Q: Is a mushroom living? You answer: not living.
Lesson line: mushrooms grow and need food.
examples.a: Corrected: living.

examples.q: Q: Which is NOT living? rock / dog / seedling / moss
examples.a: rock - it never grows or eats.
steps: Test each against the four jobs.
Choose the one with no jobs.

examples.q: Q: Why is a fallen leaf not living now? Because it stopped growing.
examples.a: A reason, not a label.
steps: Write it in a full sentence.

workbook.prompt: Answer the six practice questions on living and non-living.
workbook.answer: Six answers, all recorded before you check anything.

workbook.prompt: Check each answer against the lesson and tick the ones that agree.
workbook.answer: Ticks beside every answer the lesson supports.

workbook.prompt: Rewrite any answer the lesson disagrees with, with the reason.
workbook.answer: Corrected answers, each with the lesson line that proves it.

workbook.prompt: Write ONE question you still have about living things.
workbook.answer: A real open question in your own words - no filler.

juniper_w1_hist2.title: Helpers from Memory
juniper_w1_hist2.summary: Answer five community-helpers questions from memory, then fix two.
juniper_w1_hist2.subject: history

content.explain: Memory work has two halves: recall first, then check. Answer all FIVE questions from memory before you open the lesson - the struggle of pulling the answer out is what builds the memory. Only then check the lesson, find the two you got wrong, and rewrite them correctly. Fixing mistakes after recall is far stronger than reading the answers first.

examples.q:
Q: Who puts out fires? You write: firefighter.
Check: correct.
examples.a: Keep it, move on.

examples.q:
Q: Who fixes a leaking pipe? You write: plumber.
Check: correct.
examples.a: Keep it.

examples.q:
Q: Who raises the stop sign? You write: librarian.
Check: wrong - it is the crossing guard.
examples.a: Fix: crossing guard.

workbook.prompt: Answer five community-helpers questions from memory.
workbook.answer: Five answers written before the lesson is opened.

workbook.prompt: Open the lesson and check all five answers.
workbook.answer: Five ticks or crosses, marked honestly.

workbook.prompt: Fix the two you got wrong, with the correct answer written out.
workbook.answer: Two corrected answers written in full.

workbook.prompt: Say ONE thing each fixed helper does.
workbook.answer: A one-sentence job description for each helper you missed.

juniper_w1_cod2.title: Change Two Blocks
juniper_w1_cod2.summary: Change two blocks so the sprite does something new, then run it again.
juniper_w1_cod2.subject: coding

content.explain: Today you edit an existing program instead of starting over. Choose two blocks to change - a number, an order, or a whole block - and write down what you expect to be DIFFERENT before you run. Then run it. If the result matches your prediction, you understand the blocks. If it does not, read the blocks again and update your understanding, not your luck.

examples.q: Change move 5 steps to move 10 steps.
examples.a: The sprite travels twice as far.

examples.q: Swap say hello and move 5 steps.
examples.a: The sprite moves before it talks.

examples.q: Add turn 15 degrees after the move.
examples.a: The sprite now curves instead of going straight.

workbook.prompt: Choose two blocks and change them.
workbook.answer: Two deliberate edits, written down before running.

workbook.prompt: Write what you predict will be different.
workbook.answer: A prediction naming the change you expect on screen.

workbook.prompt: Run the program and check the prediction.
workbook.answer: A note saying whether the prediction held.

workbook.prompt: Run it a second time to confirm it behaves the same way.
workbook.answer: Two runs with the same result - programs are predictable.

juniper_w1_l3.title: Place Value Magic
juniper_w1_l3.summary: Thousands, hundreds, tens, ones — know what each digit is worth.
juniper_w1_l3.subject: math

content.explain: Every digit in a number is worth something based on where it sits. In 2,714 the 2 means 2,000, the 7 means 700, the 1 means 10, and the 4 means 4. Read from the right: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands. Say each value out loud.
examples:
6,205, digit by digit:
6 = 6,000
2 = 200
0 = 0 (the tens place is empty)
5 = 5

3,417:
The 4 sits in the hundreds place,
so the 4 means 400.

practice.question: In 6,205, which digit is in the tens place?
practice.hint: Count places from the right: ones, then tens.
practice.praise: Right! The tens place holds the 0.

practice.question: What is the value of the 5 in 2,580?
practice.hint: Find the 5, then ask which place it sits in.
practice.praise: Correct! The 5 is in the hundreds place, so it means 500.

practice.question: What does the 4 mean in 4,126?
practice.hint: It is the first digit on the left of a 4-digit number.
practice.praise: Yes! The 4 is in the thousands place, so it means 4,000.

practice.question: In 8,345, which digit is in the hundreds place?
practice.hint: Count three places in from the right: ones, tens, hundreds.
practice.praise: Nice! 3 sits in the hundreds place.

workbook.prompt: Write the value of every digit in 6,205.
Write a four-digit number with a 7 in the hundreds place.
workbook.answer: Any number where the hundreds digit is 7, e.g. 3,745.

workbook.prompt: Draw place-value blocks for 3 hundreds, 4 tens and 1 one.
workbook.answer: Blocks totalling 341, labelled hundreds, tens, ones.

workbook.prompt: Write 3,417 in words.
workbook.answer: Three thousand, four hundred seventeen.

juniper_w1_wr1.title: Three Sentences in Order
juniper_w1_wr1.summary: Tell what happened in the passage in three ordered sentences.
juniper_w1_wr1.subject: writing

content.explain: Writing in sequence means each sentence must depend on the one before it. Sentence one sets the scene or names the first event, sentence two carries the action forward, sentence three closes it. Use order words - first, then, finally - only when they are TRUE. After writing, read the three sentences aloud: if your voice stumbles, the order is wrong somewhere.

examples.q: First Maya looked for her book. Then the librarian found it. Finally Maya shared it with Ben.
examples.a: Three sentences, clear order.

examples.q: 'Finally' used before 'Then' - the reader trips.
examples.a: Swap the two sentences.

examples.q: Sentence 2 tells a detail not in the passage.
examples.a: Cut it - writing must stay inside the text.
steps: Ask: is it in the passage?

workbook.prompt: Write sentence 1: the first thing that happened.
workbook.answer: One sentence naming the first event, in your own words.

workbook.prompt: Write sentence 2: what happened next.
workbook.answer: A second sentence that follows from the first.

workbook.prompt: Write sentence 3: how it ended.
workbook.answer: A closing sentence that finishes the story.

workbook.prompt: Read all three aloud and fix any stumble.
workbook.answer: A read-aloud check, with one reorder if needed.

juniper_w1_sp2.title: Dictation and Self-Correction
juniper_w1_sp2.summary: Write all ten words from memory, then fix misses in a new colour.
juniper_w1_sp2.subject: spelling

content.explain: Dictation means your grown-up says the word and you write it without looking. Sit up tall, hear the whole word, say it in a chunk, then write it. When the list is finished, check every word against the printed list. Any word you missed gets rewritten in a NEW colour - nothing is erased. Corrections in colour show your brain exactly which letters it skipped.

examples.q:
You hear: plan
You write: plan
Check: p-l-a-n matches the list.
examples.a: Correct as written.
steps: Write it, then check letter by letter.

examples.q:
You hear: chick, you write: chik.
Check fails at the ending.
examples.a: Fix in a new colour: chick.

examples.q: Why a new colour instead of an eraser?
examples.a: So you can see what you keep getting wrong and practise that word harder.
steps: Review the colour before the next dictation.

workbook.prompt: Write all ten words from memory as your grown-up reads them.
workbook.answer: Ten words written from dictation, none erased.

workbook.prompt: Check each word against the printed list and tick the correct ones.
workbook.answer: Ticks beside every correct word.

workbook.prompt: Rewrite each missed word in a new colour.
workbook.answer: Every miss rewritten in a different colour, original left in place.

workbook.prompt: Write the two words you missed MOST three times each.
workbook.answer: Three clean repetitions of each hardest word.

juniper_w1_sci3.title: Draw and Label Four Examples
juniper_w1_sci3.summary: Draw or build examples and label four of them.
juniper_w1_sci3.subject: science

content.explain: Drawing science is a way of thinking. Draw four things from this week - two living, two non-living - and add a LABEL under each one. A good label is a short phrase that says why it belongs in its group: grows, never eats, was alive once. Labels turn a picture into evidence, and evidence is what a scientist uses to be sure.

examples.q: Draw a sunflower. Label: grows toward the light.
examples.a: Living - it grows and responds.
steps: Write the job as a label.

examples.q: Draw a spoon. Label: never eats or grows.
examples.a: Non-living.

examples.q: Draw a shell. Label: an animal left it behind.
examples.a: Once living, now not living.

workbook.prompt: Draw two living things and label each one.
workbook.answer: Two drawings with labels naming a job each one does.

workbook.prompt: Draw two non-living things and label each one.
workbook.answer: Two drawings with labels naming why each is not alive.

workbook.prompt: Add a third label that says WHY your group is correct.
workbook.answer: One group-level reason written under the pair.

workbook.prompt: Read your four labels back to your grown-up.
workbook.answer: Four labels read aloud, each one making sense on its own.

juniper_w1_hist3.title: Timeline and Map Labels
juniper_w1_hist3.summary: Add four labels to the timeline or map, then read them back.
juniper_w1_hist3.subject: history

content.explain: Labels are how historians keep track of where and when. Add FOUR labels to the community helpers timeline or outline map: the helper's name, the place they work, the tool they use, and the person they help. When you are done, read the four labels back without looking at the lesson. Reading your own writing aloud is the fastest way to catch a label that does not quite fit.

examples.q: Label: crossing guard | place: the corner | tool: stop sign | helps: children crossing.
examples.a: Four labels that fit together.

examples.q: Label: plumber | place: houses | tool: wrench | helps: anyone with a leak.
examples.a: Four matching labels.

examples.q: A label that reads 'the one with the truck' - is that a good label?
examples.a: No: it is vague. Rewrite it as the specific helper and tool.

workbook.prompt: Add four labels to the timeline or map.
workbook.answer: Four labels, one per slot: helper, place, tool, who is helped.

workbook.prompt: Read all four labels back without looking.
workbook.answer: Four labels recalled aloud from your own page.

workbook.prompt: Fix any label that was vague or did not fit.
workbook.answer: Rewritten labels that name something specific.

workbook.prompt: Tell your grown-up what each label means in one sentence.
workbook.answer: Four one-sentence explanations.

juniper_w1_cod3.title: Add a Repeat Block
juniper_w1_cod3.summary: Wrap the move in a repeat so it runs three times.
juniper_w1_cod3.subject: coding

content.explain: A repeat block runs the blocks inside it a set number of times. Today you wrap move 5 steps in repeat 3 times, so the sprite travels 15 steps without you writing three move blocks. Count the blocks INSIDE the loop, not the loop itself: one move block plus one repeat block is only two blocks, but it runs three moves.

examples.q:
repeat 3 times: move 5 steps
Runs: 5, 10, 15.
examples.a: 15 steps total.

examples.q:
repeat 2 times: move 5 steps
Runs: 5, 10.
examples.a: 10 steps total.

examples.q: You put the wait block OUTSIDE the loop by mistake.
examples.a: The sprite waits once instead of three times.

workbook.prompt: Wrap your move block in a repeat set to 3 times.
workbook.answer: A loop with exactly one move block inside, set to 3.

workbook.prompt: Predict the total number of steps before you run it.
workbook.answer: A written total: 3 x 5 = 15 steps.

workbook.prompt: Run it and count the steps on screen.
workbook.answer: An observed total matching or not matching the prediction.

workbook.prompt: Change the number inside repeat to 2 and re-predict.
workbook.answer: A new prediction: 10 steps, then a run that confirms it.

juniper_w1_l4.title: Adding Big Numbers
juniper_w1_l4.summary: Stack and add multi-digit numbers with regrouping.
juniper_w1_l4.subject: math

content.explain: Stack the numbers so the ones line up under the ones. Add the ones first, then the tens, then the hundreds. If a column adds to 10 or more, regroup: write the ones digit and carry the ten. Check it once more from the top.
examples:
268 + 145:
Ones: 8 + 5 = 13 (write 3, carry 1)
Tens: 6 + 4 + 1 = 11 (write 1, carry 1)
Hundreds: 2 + 1 + 1 = 4
Answer: 413

579 + 264:
Ones: 9 + 4 = 13 (write 3, carry 1)
Tens: 7 + 6 + 1 = 14 (write 4, carry 1)
Hundreds: 5 + 2 + 1 = 8
Answer: 843

Checking 413:
413 - 145 should give back 268.
If it does, the sum is right.

practice.hint: 8 + 5 is 13, so carry 1 into the tens column.
Add the ones first: 9 + 4 = 13, carry the 1.
6 + 7 = 13, so write 3 and carry 1 into the tens.

practice.question: What is the ones digit of 482 + 319?
practice.hint: Only add the ones column: 2 + 9.
practice.praise: Nice! 2 + 9 = 11, so the ones digit is 1.

workbook.prompt: Add 268 + 145 and show your regrouping.
workbook.answer: 413 - ones 8+5=13 write 3 carry 1; tens 6+4+1=11; hundreds 2+1+1=4.

workbook.prompt: Add 579 + 264 and show your regrouping.
Add four two-digit numbers: 23 + 19 + 34 + 16.
workbook.answer: 92 - add the ones first, then the tens.

workbook.prompt: Check one answer by subtracting back.
workbook.answer: For 413 - 145 the result must be 268 for the sum to be right.

juniper_w1_rd3.title: Retell in Order, Then Why
juniper_w1_rd3.summary: Four sentences to retell the passage, then two why-questions.
juniper_w1_rd3.subject: reading

content.explain: A retelling is not a summary of everything - it is the story in the right order. Write four sentences: what happened first, then what happened next, then the turning point, then the end. After that, answer two WHY questions. A why-answer always starts with a reason, usually because, and it must come from the passage rather than from your head.

examples.q:
Sentence 1: Maya went to the library.
Sentence 2: The big book was missing.
Sentence 3: The librarian found it under the newspapers.
Sentence 4: Maya shared with Ben.
examples.a: Four sentences in story order.

examples.q: Why did Maya choose a different story? Because she gave the book back to Ben.
examples.a: A reason sentence that starts with because.

examples.q: Why does the passage say sharing made the room friendly? Because Ben waved at her the next week.
examples.a: A proof sentence taken from the text.

workbook.prompt: Write sentence 1 of your retelling.
workbook.answer: One sentence naming the first event of the passage.

workbook.prompt: Write sentence 2 in order.
workbook.answer: One sentence naming what happened next - no events out of order.

workbook.prompt: Write sentences 3 and 4.
workbook.answer: The turning point and the ending, in that order.

workbook.prompt: Answer one why-question with a because-sentence.
workbook.answer: A complete because-sentence whose reason is in the passage.

juniper_w1_sp3.title: Cover, Write, Check the Five Hardest
juniper_w1_sp3.summary: Pick the five that trip you, then re-test yourself once.
juniper_w1_sp3.subject: spelling

content.explain: You already know most of the list, so spend this block only on the five hardest words. Look at the word, cover it with your hand, write it from memory, then lift your hand and check every letter. If a letter is wrong, fix it and cover-write it again. When all five are clean, close the list and re-test yourself once from the beginning - that second test is what moves the word into long memory.

examples.q:
Word: blast
Cover. Write: blast. Check: b-l-a-s-t. All five letters match.
examples.a: Correct on the first try.

examples.q:
Word: swim, you write: swimm.
Extra m found.
examples.a: Fix to swim, then cover-write it again.

examples.q: Re-test: all five clean without looking.
examples.a: The word has moved into long memory.

workbook.prompt: Choose the five hardest words from this week's list and write them down.
workbook.answer: Five words you actually find hard, not the five easiest.

workbook.prompt: Cover and write each of the five, then check every letter.
workbook.answer: Five cover-writes with checks marked correct or corrected.

workbook.prompt: Fix any wrong word and cover-write it once more.
workbook.answer: Each fixed word rewritten correctly after the correction.

workbook.prompt: Re-test yourself once from memory and tick every clean word.
workbook.answer: Five ticks from a closed-list test - no peeks.

juniper_w1_sci4.title: The Diagram with Five Labels
juniper_w1_sci4.summary: Draw the diagram, label five parts, explain two of them aloud.
juniper_w1_sci4.subject: science

content.explain: A diagram organises what you know into one page. Draw a scene that holds living and non-living things together - a garden, a pond, a sidewalk - and attach FIVE labels across it. Then choose two labels and explain them out loud in full sentences. If you cannot explain a label without looking, the label is not finished yet.

examples.q: Garden scene with labels: snail, stone, leaf, sunlight, rain.
examples.a: Five labels, three living-ish and two non-living.

examples.q: Label: snail - living. Say: The snail is living because it eats and moves on its own.
examples.a: A complete spoken explanation.

examples.q: Label: stone - not living. Say: The stone never grows or eats.
examples.a: A complete spoken explanation.
steps: Name what it does NOT do.

workbook.prompt: Draw one scene containing at least three different things.
workbook.answer: A single scene with three or more separate objects drawn clearly.

workbook.prompt: Add five labels across the diagram.
workbook.answer: Five distinct labels attached to five different parts.

workbook.prompt: Explain two of your labels to a parent in full sentences.
workbook.answer: Two spoken sentences, each naming a job or a missing job.

workbook.prompt: Circle the label you found hardest to explain and improve it.
workbook.answer: One rewritten label that you can now say without help.

juniper_w1_cv1.title: Four Symbols of Our Country
juniper_w1_cv1.summary: Name four symbols and what each one stands for.
juniper_w1_cv1.subject: civics

content.explain: A symbol is a real object that stands for a bigger idea. The flag is cloth, but it stands for the nation and everyone in it. Today you name FOUR symbols and say what each one stands for - not what it is made of, but what it means. Knowing the difference between a thing and what it stands for is the whole skill of civics.

examples.q: The flag: cloth and colour, but it stands for the nation itself.
examples.a: Meaning, not material.

examples.q: The Statue of Liberty: a statue, but it stands for welcome and freedom.
examples.a: An idea, not just a landmark.

examples.q: The bald eagle: a bird, but it stands for strength and freedom.
examples.a: A national emblem.
steps: Name the quality it stands for.

workbook.prompt: Name four symbols of our country.
workbook.answer: Four symbols written out - flag, Statue of Liberty, bald eagle, national anthem.

workbook.prompt: Write what each symbol stands for.
workbook.answer: One meaning per symbol - an idea, not a material.

workbook.prompt: Tell your grown-up two of them without looking.
workbook.answer: Two spoken explanations from memory.

workbook.prompt: Draw one symbol and write its meaning under it.
workbook.answer: A labelled drawing whose caption names the idea it stands for.

juniper_w1_cod4.title: Find the Block That Stops It Early
juniper_w1_cod4.summary: Run it, spot the one bad block, fix it, run it again.
juniper_w1_cod4.subject: coding

content.explain: Debugging is reading, not guessing. Run the program, notice where it stops early, and then read EVERY block from the top, asking what each one actually does. The bad block is usually doing exactly what it says - it is just in the wrong place or has the wrong number. Fix ONE block at a time and re-run after each fix, so you always know which change solved it.

examples.q: A pause block sits inside the loop, so the sprite crawls.
examples.a: Move the pause out of the loop.

examples.q: The sprite stops after 3 steps but should do 5.
examples.a: Check the number inside move.

examples.q: You changed three blocks at once and it works now.
examples.a: Bad practice - you do not know which fix mattered.

workbook.prompt: Run the program and write down WHERE it stops early.
workbook.answer: A specific spot: which block, which step.

workbook.prompt: Read every block from the top and write what each one does.
workbook.answer: Five short notes, one per block, in order.

workbook.prompt: Fix the single block that causes the problem.
workbook.answer: One edit only, aimed at the cause you identified.

workbook.prompt: Run it twice to prove the fix holds.
workbook.answer: Two clean runs with the intended behaviour both times.

juniper_w1_lit1.title: Our Reader: Character, Setting, Problem
juniper_w1_lit1.summary: Read 15 minutes of the class reader, then name the character, the setting and the problem in your own words.
juniper_w1_lit1.subject: literature

content.explain: Literature is a story written to be read and felt, not mined for facts. While you read a chapter, hold three questions in your head: who is this about (the main character), where and when does it happen (the setting), and what is going wrong or in the way (the problem). Read the chapter once for pleasure, then stop and answer the three questions out loud before you write anything. The problem usually shows up early — it is what keeps you turning pages.

examples.q:
Chapter 2: the shelf where the big book should be is empty.
What is the problem?
examples.a: The book is missing, so somebody has to find it or fix it.
steps: Say who the chapter is about.

examples.q:
You read: The rain hammered the roof while she waited inside.
What is the setting?
examples.a: Inside the library, on a rainy day.

examples.q: Why does the setting matter here?
examples.a: Being stuck inside is why she keeps reading and why she notices the empty shelf.
steps: Ask what the place forces the character to do.
Ask what would change if the place were different.

practice.question: Which of these is a SETTING?
practice.hint: Setting answers where and when.
practice.praise: Yes! Place and time together.

practice.question: A problem in a story is…
options: something the character must deal with
practice.hint: Something is wrong or in the way for the character.
practice.praise: Right — the character has something to handle.

workbook.prompt: Write the character, the setting and the problem from today’s chapter in three lines.
workbook.answer: Three lines: a name (or description) of the main character, a place and time, and what is going wrong.

workbook.prompt: Copy one sentence that shows the problem without saying "problem".
workbook.answer: A quoted line from the chapter where something is missing, wrong or in the way.

workbook.prompt: Write one question you still have about the chapter.
workbook.answer: An open question about what happens next, the character’s choice, or the missing thing.

workbook.prompt: Tell a grown-up what happened in the chapter in 30 seconds, without looking.
workbook.answer: A spoken retell covering who, where and what is going wrong.

test.title: Week 1 Test — Launch & Baseline
test.note: Drawn from Juniper's mapped week-1 lessons (skip-counting, multiplication 2-5, place value, adding) plus the week-1 reading, spelling and science blocks.

questions.why: Zero groups means nothing to add — any number times 0 is 0.
Three groups of 4: 4, 8, 12.
Count by 5s five times: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25.

questions.q: Which list counts by 2s?
questions.why: Each number is exactly 2 more than the one before it.

questions.q: What number comes next?  5, 10, 15, ___
questions.why: Add 5 to the last number you said.

questions.q: What is the value of the 5 in 2,580?
questions.why: Find the 5, then name its place — it sits in the hundreds, so it means 500.

questions.q: In 8,345, which digit is in the hundreds place?
questions.why: Count places from the right: ones, tens, hundreds — the 3 is third.

questions.q: Because the library was closed, Sam read on the steps. Why did Sam read on the steps?
questions.why: The sentence starts with Because, and the answer sits right there in the text — look again before you guess.

questions.q: Which word is spelled correctly?
questions.why: Say it in chunks and watch the middle: a friend comes first, spelled f-r-i-e-n-d.

questions.q: Which of these is living?
questions.why: A living thing grows, eats and moves — a rock and a chair do none of those.

items.name: a dog
items.why: It eats, grows and breathes.

items.name: a rose bush
items.why: It grows and needs water and sunlight.

items.name: a mushroom
items.why: It grows and needs food to live.

items.name: a goldfish
items.why: It breathes, eats and grows.

items.name: a seedling
items.why: It is growing right now.

items.name: an oak tree
items.why: It grows, drinks water and breathes through its leaves.

items.name: an egg
items.why: A baby bird grows inside it and it needs warmth.

items.name: moss on a wall
items.why: It grows and needs dampness to survive.

items.name: a rock
items.why: It never eats, grows or breathes.

items.name: a spoon
items.why: It is a tool made of metal and it never grows.

items.name: a cloud
items.why: It is weather, not alive, and it does not breathe.

items.name: a chair
items.why: It was built by people and it is not alive.

items.name: a puddle
items.why: It is water and water is not alive.

items.name: a shoe
items.why: It does not eat, grow or breathe.

items.name: a dead leaf
items.why: It was living once, but it has stopped growing.

items.name: a candle
items.why: Wax is not alive, even when the flame moves.

items.name: a bicycle
items.why: It moves only when a rider pushes it.

items.name: a shell
items.why: The animal left it behind and it never grows.

sets.title: Getting help when someone is hurt
Returning a library book
events: You put it in your bag
You hand it to the librarian
The librarian stamps the return card

sets.title: A crossing guard at the corner
events: The guard raises the stop sign

sets.title: The plumber fixes a leak
events: The plumber turns off the water

items.q: Which community helper puts out fires?
items.hint: Look for the helper with the bright red truck and the hose.

items.q: Who brings the mail to our street every day?
items.hint: This helper walks the same route after breakfast.

items.q: Who helps children cross the street at the corner?
items.hint: This helper carries a stop sign and wears a bright vest.

items.q: Who should you call if a pipe is leaking?
items.hint: This helper carries a wrench and fixes water pipes.

items.q: Where do you return a library book?
items.hint: This person works at the front desk of the library.

items.q: Who arrives in an ambulance when someone is hurt?
items.hint: This helper rides in the ambulance and knows first aid.

items.q: What does a crossing guard do first when buses arrive?
items.hint: The sign must go up before any child crosses.

items.q: Which helper do you ask when the toilet will not flush?
items.hint: This helper fixes water problems in a house.

items.q: Who checks the return bin at the library?
items.hint: She works beside the shelves and the stamp.

items.q: Why do community helpers practise their steps?
options: So they can use them without guessing
items.hint: The passage says helpers learn, practise, then use the steps.

items.question: Which block makes the sprite move forward?
items.hint: Sprites move when a MOVE block runs. The number tells how far.

items.question: A sprite has these blocks in order: say hello, move 5 steps, wait 2 seconds. Which runs FIRST?
items.hint: Blocks run from the top down, one after another.
items.praise: Yes - the top block runs first.

items.question: How many steps does this run?  move 5 steps, move 5 steps, move 5 steps
items.hint: Add the steps: 5 + 5 + 5.

items.question: You press run and nothing moves. What should you do FIRST?
options: Read the blocks from the top
items.hint: Debugging starts with reading the blocks, not guessing.
items.praise: Yes - read the blocks from the top.

items.question: Which block makes a sprite stand still for a moment?
items.hint: A WAIT block pauses the sprite without stopping the program.

items.question: Which of these is a BLOCK you could drag out?
items.hint: Blocks are short, exact instructions the computer understands.
items.praise: Yes - move 5 steps is a real block.

items.question: Change one block so the sprite moves 10 steps instead of 5. What do you change?
options: The number inside the move block
items.hint: The number inside a block is a value you can edit.

items.question: Your sprite moves forward but you wanted it to move back. Which block fits better?
items.hint: A negative number moves in the opposite direction.

items.question: Two blocks are in the wrong order: move 5 steps then say hello. You want the sprite to talk first. What do you do?
options: Drag say hello above move 5 steps
items.hint: Order matters: the top block always runs first.
items.praise: Yes - drag say hello to the top.

items.question: Which change makes the sprite do something NEW?
options: Add a turn block after the move
items.hint: A new block gives the sprite new behaviour.
items.praise: Yes - a turn block changes where it goes.

items.question: You add a wait block between two moves. What happens now?
options: The sprite pauses between the moves
The sprite moves twice as fast
items.hint: WAIT pauses the program at that point.
items.praise: Yes - it pauses between the moves.

items.question: You press run, then stop, then run again. Why does the sprite start from the beginning?
options: Run always starts at the first block
items.hint: Programs start at the top block every time you press run.
items.praise: Yes - run starts at the first block.

items.question: Which block would you add so the sprite moves 5 steps three times?
items.hint: A repeat block runs the blocks inside it again and again.

items.question: repeat 3 times wraps move 5 steps. How far does the sprite travel?
items.hint: The move block runs 3 times: 3 x 5 = 15.

items.question: Where do the blocks go that should be repeated?
items.hint: Only blocks inside the mouth of the repeat are repeated.

items.question: repeat 2 times: move 5 steps. How many steps in total?
items.hint: 2 x 5 = 10 steps.

items.question: What does the number inside repeat tell the sprite?
items.hint: That number is the number of times.
items.praise: Yes - how many times to repeat.

items.question: Which is the shorter way to move 5 steps four times?
items.hint: One repeat block replaces many copies.
items.praise: Yes - one repeat block does the job.

items.question: You wrote repeat 10 times but meant 3. What do you do?
options: Change the number inside repeat to 3
items.hint: The value inside the block is editable.

items.question: The sprite stops early. What is the BEST way to find the problem?
options: Read each block from the top and check it
items.hint: Debugging means reading carefully, not guessing.
items.praise: Yes - read the blocks from the top.

items.question: A pause block sits in the middle of your repeat. What should you do?
options: Move it out of the repeat if you did not mean to pause
items.hint: Unwanted pauses inside a loop slow everything down.
items.praise: Yes - move it out of the repeat.

items.question: Your program runs but the sprite goes the wrong way. What do you change?
options: The direction or sign in the move block
items.hint: Direction lives in the move value.

items.question: Which check happens BEFORE you press run?
options: Read the blocks in order and picture the result
items.hint: Good coders predict before they run.

items.question: You fix a block and run it again. Why?
items.hint: A fix is only a fix after you test it.
items.praise: Yes - run it again to prove the fix.

items.question: Your sprite moves 5 steps but should move 3. What is wrong?
options: The number in the move block
items.hint: The value inside the block is wrong.

items.question: Which sentence starts with a capital letter and ends correctly?
items.hint: A sentence starts with a capital and ends with a period.
items.praise: Yes - capital first word, period at the end.

items.question: Which sentence ends with a question mark?
items.hint: A question needs a question mark.

items.question: Which word must start with a capital letter?
items.hint: Names of people always start with a capital.

items.question: Which sentence is written correctly?
items.hint: Capital first letter, small letters after, period at the end.

items.question: Which sentence shows strong feeling with the right end mark?
items.hint: Strong feeling can end with a period or an exclamation point.

items.question: Which sentence is missing its end mark?
items.hint: Every sentence needs a mark at the very end.

items.question: Which sentence capitalizes the first word correctly?
items.hint: Only the first word and names need capitals here.
items.praise: Yes - My cat sleeps all day.

items.question: Which is a complete sentence?
items.hint: A complete sentence tells a whole idea and ends with a mark.

items.question: Which sentence ends with an exclamation point?
items.hint: Strong feeling or a warning ends with an exclamation point.

items.question: Which sentence uses capitals correctly?
items.hint: Days of the week always start with a capital.
items.praise: Yes - On Monday we baked bread.

items.question: Which sentence needs a question mark at the end?
items.hint: A sentence that asks something ends with a question mark.
items.praise: Yes - Do you want an apple?

items.question: Which word is NOT capitalized correctly?
items.hint: The first word of a sentence must be a capital.
items.praise: Yes - 'my friend Ava' should be 'My friend Ava'.

items.question: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
items.hint: It asks a question, so it needs a question mark.

items.question: Which title should start with a capital?
items.hint: Every important word in a title starts with a capital.
items.praise: Yes - My Trip to the Lake.

items.question: Which sentence ends correctly?
items.hint: A polite request is a statement and ends with a period.

items.question: Which sentence is written the BEST way?
items.hint: Capital first letter, normal letters after, period at the end.

items.question: Which sentence tells what happened FIRST in a story about a lost book?
options: Then I found it in the hall.
So I put it on the shelf.
items.hint: The first event comes before all the others.
items.praise: Yes - that is the first event.

items.question: Which sentence gives the clearest detail?
options: The dog ran across the yard.
items.hint: A strong sentence tells what and where.
items.praise: Yes - it names the action and the place.

items.question: Which order of three sentences retells a reading session?
options: First I read it. Then I answered. Last I checked.
Last I checked. First I read it. Then I answered.
Then I answered. Last I checked. First I read it.
items.hint: Order words first, then, last must match the events.
items.praise: Yes - the order words line up.

items.question: Which sentence is a complete thought?
items.hint: A complete sentence has a subject and a verb and ends with a mark.
items.praise: Yes - that is a complete sentence.

items.question: Which detail should NOT go in a retelling of the passage?
items.hint: Only details from the passage belong in a retelling.
items.praise: Yes - lunch is not in the story.

items.question: Which sentence retells the passage in order?
options: Maya lost the book, asked the librarian, then shared with Ben.
Ben lost the book, Maya hid it, the librarian left.
The librarian wrote a book, Ben read it, Maya went home.
Maya bought a book, Ben bought a book, they read.
items.hint: Follow the events exactly as the passage tells them.

items.question: Which word best starts a WHY sentence?
items.hint: A why sentence usually starts with because.

items.question: Which sentence answers a WHY question about the passage?
options: Because the return bin was under the newspapers.
items.hint: A why answer gives a reason, not just a fact.

items.question: Which sentence is written in your OWN words?
options: Maya felt glad when Ben waved at her.
Maya loved Tuesdays because that was library day.
Maya always chose one big book and one funny book.
The librarian checked the return bin.
items.hint: Your own words retell the idea without copying it.
items.praise: Yes - that is in your own words.

items.question: Which sentence needs a detail added to be complete?
options: She liked the funny book about the bear.
items.hint: Who is she, and what did she like?

items.question: Which is the BEST first sentence for a story about spring?
options: The crocuses pushed through the cold dirt.
Spring happened and then other things.
items.hint: Start with a picture the reader can see.
items.praise: Yes - that shows the reader the scene.

items.question: Which sentence ends a 3-sentence retelling best?
options: That is why the story ends happily.
items.hint: A good ending wraps the idea up.

items.question: Which sentence uses an order word correctly?
items.hint: Order words go at the start of the sentence, then say what happened.
items.praise: Yes - First I underlined three words.

items.question: Which sentence would a reader understand BEST?
options: The crossing guard raised her red sign.
The thing was at the place.
items.hint: Name the person, the object and the action.

items.question: Which sentence belongs in a HOW paragraph about the library visit?
options: We checked out the books by scanning the card.
items.hint: A HOW sentence explains the steps.

items.question: Which sentence should be REWRITTEN because a word is repeated?
options: The the book was on the shelf.
The book was on the shelf.
The book sat on the shelf.
A book was on the shelf.
items.hint: Read it aloud - you will hear the doubled word.

items.question: What does the flag of our country stand for?
options: The nation itself and the people in it
items.hint: The flag is the symbol of the whole country.
items.praise: Yes - the flag stands for the nation.

items.question: Which symbol welcomes people to a harbour with a torch?
items.hint: She holds a torch and stands in New York harbour.

items.question: What does the bald eagle represent?
items.hint: It is the national bird.

items.question: What is the national anthem?
items.hint: It is sung before big national events.

items.question: Why do we learn the symbols of our country?
options: So we can recognise what each one stands for
So we can pass a test only
items.hint: Each symbol carries a meaning worth knowing.
items.praise: Yes - so we know what each one means.

items.question: Which of these is a SYMBOL, not a person?
items.hint: A symbol stands for something bigger than itself.
items.praise: Yes - the flag is a symbol.

items.question: Who is a community helper in our neighbourhood?
items.hint: This helper works in our town.

items.question: What does the Pledge of Allegiance show?
options: A promise to clean the room
items.hint: It is said together at the start of the school day.

items.question: Which symbol would you see on a government building?
items.hint: Flags fly above public buildings.

items.question: What does the Statue of Liberty hold in her hand?
items.hint: Her torch lights the way.

items.question: Which statement about symbols is TRUE?
options: A symbol stands for an idea bigger than itself
A symbol is only a drawing
items.hint: Think about what a flag means to millions of people.
items.praise: Yes - symbols stand for bigger ideas.

items.question: Why do people stand when the anthem plays?
items.hint: Standing is a sign of respect.

items.question: Which group does the flag belong to?
items.hint: The whole nation shares it.

items.question: How should a flag be treated?
items.hint: Symbols are treated with care.

items.question: What do our country's symbols help us remember?
options: The ideas our country was built on
items.hint: Each symbol carries an idea from history.
items.praise: Yes - the ideas the country was built on.

items.question: Which is a symbol of our country's government?
items.hint: The Great Seal appears on official documents.

items.q: Which fact family belongs to 5, 6 and 30?
items.hint: A fact family uses one multiplication, its flip and one division.
items.praise: Yes! Three numbers, three facts, one family.

items.q: 9 x 6 = 54. Which division is in the same family?
items.hint: Divide the product by one factor to get the other.

items.q: Which fact should go in the re-learn pile?
options: The one you must count on your fingers
The one you already know cold
The one with the smallest answer
items.hint: The re-learn pile is for facts that are not automatic yet.
items.praise: Yes! Re-learn means practise it again.

items.q: What does a CAPTION tell a reader?
options: What a photo shows and where
items.hint: A caption is the short line under a photo.
items.praise: Yes! It names and locates what the photo shows.

items.q: Where do you look up the meaning of a technical word?
items.hint: Glossary words are listed in alphabetical order.
items.praise: Yes! The glossary defines the technical vocabulary.

items.q: Which sentence is the main idea of a paragraph?
options: The one the other sentences prove
The one with a number in it
items.hint: Ask what the other sentences are there to support.
items.praise: Yes! The main idea is the claim the details back up.

items.q: Which is camouflage?
options: A moth that looks like tree bark
A bear sleeping in a den
items.hint: Camouflage is about not being seen.
items.praise: Yes! Looking like the bark hides the moth.

items.q: Why does an animal hibernate?
options: To survive a season with almost no food
items.hint: Think about what winter removes from the habitat.
items.praise: Yes! Slowing down stretches a thin food supply.

items.q: Migration is best described as...
options: A long seasonal trip to a better place
items.hint: Migration involves travel.
items.praise: Yes! The animal moves instead of waiting.

items.q: Which comes first on a town timeline?
items.hint: Timelines run from the past forward.

items.q: Why did early towns grow near rivers?
options: Water, food and a road for trade
items.hint: Think about what a river gives and what it carries.
items.praise: Yes! A river is a pantry and a road at once.

items.q: Who does a historian thank for a fact?
items.hint: Every historical claim rests on a source.
items.praise: Yes! Name the source and you can defend the claim.

items.hint: Ones 5+9=14 carry 1, tens 7+4+1=12 carry 1.
items.praise: Yes! Four columns, three carries, one answer.

items.q: Which step comes first in a four-digit sum?
items.hint: Always start at the right-hand end.
items.praise: Yes! Right to left, every time.

items.hint: Add the thousands digits and keep the three zeros.
items.praise: Yes! Five thousands and three thousands make eight.

items.q: Which word best completes: they _____ their position rather than measured it?
items.hint: Read the contrast: guessing versus measuring.
items.praise: Yes! The sentence sets guessing against measuring.

items.q: Sequence words such as first, then and finally help a reader...
items.hint: Think about what order words do.
items.praise: Yes! They are the skeleton of informational text.

items.q: Where do you check a detail you half remember?
items.hint: The text is the evidence.
items.praise: Yes! Point to the line that proves it.

items.q: What causes the seasons?
items.hint: Think about which way the Earth leans.
items.praise: Yes! The tilt changes the angle of the light.

items.q: Weather means...
options: what the air is doing today
items.hint: Weather is short-term.
items.praise: Yes! Day to day is weather.

items.q: A pattern is best found by...
options: recording the same measure over many days
items.hint: Patterns need repeated records.
items.praise: Yes! Tally it, graph it, then read it.

items.q: Explorers first crossed the Atlantic because they wanted...
items.hint: Trade drove the voyages.
items.praise: Yes! The new land was a means, not the plan.

items.q: Which explorer's crew completed the first trip around the world?
items.hint: Magellan died on the way; his crew finished.
items.praise: Yes! The crew completed what the captain began.

items.q: A dated voyage line on a map tells a historian...
options: when a place became known to that country
items.hint: Dates are the point of the line.
items.praise: Yes! Date plus route is a checkable claim.

items.q: Round 65 to the nearest 10.
items.hint: Five or more rounds up.
items.praise: Yes! The ones digit is 5, so round up.

items.q: Round 34 to the nearest 10.
items.hint: Four or less stays.

items.q: Which estimate is closest to 71 + 18?
items.hint: Round each number first.

items.q: In this passage, a front is...
options: the boundary between two air masses
items.hint: The sentence about arguing air masses gives it away.

items.q: Crowded isobars tell you the wind is...
items.hint: Spacing on the map carries meaning.
items.praise: Yes! Close loops mean a strong difference.

items.q: A diagram is...
options: a labelled picture that carries real information
items.hint: Read the labels and leader lines.
items.praise: Yes! Never decoration, always a shortcut.

items.q: A rain gauge measures...
items.hint: Think of what collects in it.
items.praise: Yes! It collects and measures rainfall.

items.q: A wind vane shows...
items.hint: It points into the wind.

items.q: A barometer reads...
items.hint: Falling pressure hints at a change.
items.praise: Yes! Pressure is the forecasting workhorse.

items.q: A route line on a map is most useful when it carries...
items.hint: Without dates a route proves nothing.
items.praise: Yes! Date plus place is the evidence.

items.q: Why did sailing around Africa matter?
options: It opened a sea route to India's trade
items.hint: Think about what the route reached.
items.praise: Yes! It connected Europe to Indian Ocean trade.

items.q: What is a historian's first step with a route?
options: Put it in order with the others
items.hint: Order first, meaning second.

items.q: Which is the fairest check of a skill?
options: Ten items with no practice first
Ten items after an hour of drilling
items.hint: Cold testing hides nothing.
items.praise: Yes! Cold items measure what is secure.

items.hint: Ones 6+7=13 carry 1, tens 5+6+1=12 carry 1.

items.q: A skill counts as fixed when...
options: you get it right twice a day apart
items.hint: One success can be luck.
items.praise: Yes! Spaced success is the honest bar.

items.q: The reading log improved because...
options: a student named the missing piece
items.hint: Find who spoke up.
items.praise: Yes! Ari named what the log never asked for.

items.q: A personal narrative can also...
items.hint: This piece tells a story to prove something.
items.praise: Yes! Story in service of a claim.

items.q: The phrase a margin means the change was...
options: small enough to fit beside the text
items.hint: A margin is a narrow strip.
items.praise: Yes! Small enough to write beside the column.

items.q: Which animal is a mammal?
items.hint: Hair and milk are the deciding traits.
items.praise: Yes! Dolphins breathe air, have hair and feed milk.

items.q: Feathers belong to which group?
items.hint: Only one group has them.
items.praise: Yes! Feathers are unique to birds.

items.q: An amphibian typically...
options: starts in water with gills and later breathes air
items.hint: Look for the change of breathing.
items.praise: Yes! The switch from gills to lungs is the marker.

items.q: The best first step in a review is...
options: rebuild it from memory, then check
items.hint: Retrieval shows you the holes.

items.q: Which source is strongest for a town's founding?
options: A dated council record from that year
items.hint: Dated and close to the event wins.

items.q: Records of the past are kept so that...
options: we can trace how the town changed
items.hint: Records are evidence of change.
items.praise: Yes! That is history at town level.

items.q: Each of 4 baskets holds 6 apples. How many apples?
items.hint: Each signals equal groups.
items.praise: Yes! Four equal groups of six.

items.hint: Count by eights seven times.

items.q: Which step comes first with a word problem?
options: Find the clue that names the operation
items.hint: Choose before you compute.
items.praise: Yes! The clue decides the operation.

items.q: Proving an answer means...
options: pointing to the line in the text that supports it
items.hint: Evidence is a line you can point to.

items.q: In a literary passage, motive is...
items.hint: Motive is the reason behind the action.
items.praise: Yes! Say, want or fear gives the motive.

items.q: In practical text you should read directions...
items.hint: Instructions mean exactly what they say.
items.praise: Yes! Literal reading is the right mode.

items.q: A fair test changes...
options: only one thing at a time
items.hint: Otherwise you cannot say what caused what.

items.q: Which is a testable question?
options: Does more light make a bean plant taller?
items.hint: Look for something you can measure.
items.praise: Yes! Taller is measurable in centimetres.

items.q: Your prediction should include...
items.hint: A prediction is a claim plus why.
items.praise: Yes! The reason is the science.

items.q: The strongest defence of a historical claim is...
options: a dated source you can point to
items.hint: Evidence beats emphasis.
items.praise: Yes! Date it and show it.

items.q: Interleaving the strands on one timeline shows...
options: what happened at the same time as other events
items.hint: One axis, several strands.

items.q: Local history matters because...
options: it explains what the land and the people allowed
items.hint: Think about place.
items.praise: Yes! Geography shapes what a town can become.

items.q: 18 shared into 3 equal groups gives...
items.hint: Ask how many in each pile.
items.praise: Yes! Three piles of six make eighteen.

items.q: Which division belongs to 8 x 5 = 40?
items.hint: Dividing by one factor returns the other.

items.q: A remainder is...
options: what is left over after equal sharing
items.hint: Equal sharing does not always use everything.

items.q: A character trait is best shown by...
options: a pattern of what they do
items.hint: Look for repetition across the story.
items.praise: Yes! Repeated behaviour is the evidence.

items.q: Evidence for a trait should be...
options: a specific action or line from the story
items.hint: Quote the text, not your feeling.

items.q: Which trait word fits a character who waits in the rain for a stranger?
items.hint: They stuck to what was right.
items.praise: Yes! Doing the right thing at a cost.

items.q: The correct order for a butterfly is...
items.hint: Start with the egg.
items.praise: Yes! Each stage sets up the next.

items.q: A tadpole breathes with...
items.hint: It lives in water first.
items.praise: Yes! Gills in water, lungs on land.

items.q: The purpose of a flower in a plant's cycle is...
options: to make seeds for the next generation
items.hint: Think about what comes after the flower.
items.praise: Yes! Fruit and seed follow the flower.

items.q: An invention is most useful to a historian as...
options: dated evidence of what a society could do
items.hint: Dates are the value.

items.q: Inventions usually appear when...
options: an old answer stops being good enough
items.hint: Look for the failing predecessor.
items.praise: Yes! Need pulls the invention into being.

items.q: The failure notebook matters because it shows...
items.hint: Process, not product.
items.praise: Yes! It records what was tried and why.

items.q: In 8,345 the digit 3 stands for...
items.hint: Count the columns from the right.
items.praise: Yes! The 3 sits in the hundreds column.

items.q: Round 6,819 to the nearest ten.
items.hint: The ones digit is 9.
items.praise: Yes! Nine or more rounds the tens digit up.

items.q: Which is the largest?
items.hint: Compare hundreds first, then tens.
items.praise: Yes! The hundreds column breaks the tie.

items.q: A scale bar lets you...
options: work out real distance from map distance
items.hint: It is a ratio between paper and ground.
items.praise: Yes! Centimetres on paper become metres on the ground.

items.q: The compass rose fixes...
options: north, and therefore every other direction
items.hint: Everything else is a bearing from there.

items.q: Two sources disagree, so you...
options: record both and say which you trust, with a reason
items.hint: Silent choosing is not history.
items.praise: Yes! State the disagreement and your judgement.

items.q: Erosion means...
options: wearing away and carrying off material
items.hint: Think water, wind and ice at work.
items.praise: Yes! Worn away and moved off.

items.q: A delta forms where...
options: a river slows and drops sediment
items.hint: Slow water drops its load.
items.praise: Yes! Deposition at the river's mouth.

items.q: Which force works slowest?
items.hint: Think in centuries.
items.praise: Yes! Glaciers grind given enough time.

items.q: Old cities cluster at crossings and harbours because...
options: goods and people must pass there
items.hint: Think trade.

items.q: A region is an area that shares...
items.hint: Something in common defines it.
items.praise: Yes! Shared traits draw the line.

items.q: Physical features shaped borders because...
options: rivers and mountains are natural edges
items.hint: Nature draws first lines.
items.praise: Yes! Rivers and ranges make convenient boundaries.

items.q: A shape in 4 equal parts with 1 shaded shows...
items.hint: One part out of four.
items.praise: Yes! One of four equal parts.

items.q: Which is larger, 1/3 or 1/5?
items.hint: Fewer parts means bigger pieces.
items.praise: Yes! Thirds are bigger than fifths.

items.q: Fractions can only be compared when...
options: the wholes are the same size
items.hint: Different wholes make comparison meaningless.

passages.title: A Story About a Lost Library Book
passages.text: Maya loved Tuesdays because that was library day. She always chose one big book and one funny book. One Tuesday the big book was missing from the shelf. Maya asked the librarian if anyone had returned it. The librarian checked the return bin and found the book under a stack of newspapers. A name tag inside the cover said it belonged to a second grader named Ben. Maya felt sorry that Ben had lost his book, so she gave it back to him and chose a different story. The next Tuesday Ben waved at her from across the reading room. Sharing the shelf made the whole room feel friendly.

passages.title: Community Helpers on Our Street
passages.text: Our street has helpers who work every day. The mail carrier walks the same route after breakfast. The crossing guard stands at the corner when the buses arrive. If a pipe bursts, the plumber brings tools to stop the water. If someone is hurt, a paramedic arrives in a bright red truck. Each helper follows steps that were taught to them. They learn the steps, they practise the steps, and then they use the steps. Knowing which helper does which job keeps our neighbourhood calm and safe.

passages.title: Living and Non-Living in the Garden
passages.text: In our garden a snail crawls over a wet stone. The snail is living because it eats, grows and moves on its own. The stone is not living, and it will never eat or grow. A fallen leaf was once living, but now it is dry and crumbly. Sunlight pours onto the plants and the plants drink it in. Rain is not living either, but living things could not survive without it. Look closely at any patch of ground and you will find both kinds of things side by side.

passages.title: The Sprite That Would Not Stop
passages.text: We built a sprite in the block editor and pressed run. The sprite moved five steps and waited for us. We added a repeat block so the sprite moved five steps three times. Then we pressed run again and the sprite ran across the whole screen. Our teacher asked us to find the one block that made it stop early. We read the blocks from the top, one at a time. The pause block was in the wrong place, so we moved it down. Debugging meant reading carefully, not guessing.
