juniper_w4_l1.title: Coding: Step by Step
juniper_w4_l1.summary: Algorithms are just lists of steps — write one for making a sandwich.
juniper_w4_l1.subject: coding

content.explain: An algorithm is just a list of steps that finishes a job. Good steps are in order, small enough to follow, and clear enough that anyone could do them. Ask yourself: if a robot followed my instructions exactly, would it work? Test your steps on a grown-up.
examples:
Make a jam sandwich:
1. Get two slices of bread.
2. Unscrew the jar lid.
3. Spread jam on one slice.
4. Screw the lid back on.
5. Put the slices together.
Debugging: if step 2 only says open the jar, a robot stalls at the lid. Add the missing step and test again.
The steps of brushing teeth: pick up the brush, put paste on it, brush, spit, rinse. Order matters.

practice.question: Your steps for a task work best when they are...
options: In the right order, clear and small
practice.hint: Think about a robot following your list exactly.
practice.praise: Yes! Steps must be in order, clear, and small.

practice.question: A friend follows your directions and goes the wrong way. What should you do?
options: Fix the unclear step and try again
practice.hint: Programmers call this debugging.
practice.praise: Right! Fix the step and test it again.

practice.question: Which is the best first step for brushing your teeth?
options: Pick up the toothbrush and put paste on it
practice.hint: A first step happens before everything else.
practice.praise: Correct! You need the brush ready first.

practice.question: In a list of steps, step 3 comes...
practice.hint: Steps run in order from start to finish.
practice.praise: Nice! Step 3 sits right between 2 and 4.

juniper_w4_l2.title: Sequences & Loops
juniper_w4_l2.summary: Put blocks in order and repeat them with a loop.
juniper_w4_l2.subject: coding

content.explain: A sequence is blocks that run one after another, from top to bottom. A loop repeats a set of blocks without rebuilding them. If you catch yourself copying the same block three times, use a loop instead. Loops count the repeats for you.
examples:
Repeat 4 times:
block A, block A, block A, block A
is the same as:
repeat 4 times: block A
One block, four runs.
Sequence: move forward, turn right, move forward. Order matters: swap two blocks and you walk into the wall.
A repeat block with 6 inside runs its blocks 6 times, then moves on.

practice.question: You need to clap 5 times. Which instruction is shorter?
practice.hint: One repeat block can replace many copies.
practice.praise: Yes! A loop does the repeating for you.

practice.question: A loop that repeats 3 times runs its blocks...
practice.hint: The number inside the loop is the count.
practice.praise: Correct! Three repeats means three runs.

practice.question: Blocks in a sequence run...
practice.hint: Sequences follow the order you see them.
practice.praise: Right! Top block first, then the next one down.

practice.question: Which block makes other blocks repeat?
practice.hint: Its name tells you what it does.
practice.praise: Nice! The repeat block loops the blocks inside it.

juniper_w4_l3.title: Science Lab Fun
juniper_w4_l3.summary: Simple experiments: sinks, floats, and changing states.
juniper_w4_l3.subject: science

content.explain: Science means asking a question and then testing it fairly. A sink-or-float test uses the same water, the same drop height, and one object at a time. Write down what you saw before you decide why. Changing one thing at a time keeps your test honest.
examples:
Test: do rocks float?
Same tub, same drop height, one object at a time.
Rock sinks, cork floats, plastic cap floats.
Big idea: lighter-for-its-size things float.
States of matter: ice melts into water when heated, and water freezes into ice when cooled. Same stuff, different state.
Fair test checklist: same water, same height, one change at a time.

practice.question: Which one most likely floats in water?
practice.hint: Think about what is lighter for its size.
practice.praise: Yes! A cork floats.

practice.question: Ice left in the sun turns into...
practice.hint: Melting turns a solid into a liquid.
practice.praise: Correct! Ice melts into water.

practice.question: You test whether a ball sinks. What must stay the same?
practice.hint: A fair test changes only one thing.
practice.praise: Right! Keep the water setup the same.

practice.question: Water boiled in a kettle becomes...
practice.hint: Heating a liquid turns it into a gas.
practice.praise: Nice! Boiling water turns into water vapour.

juniper_w4_l4.title: History Heroes
juniper_w4_l4.summary: Meet explorers and inventors — keep that 4/5 history humming.
juniper_w4_l4.subject: history

content.explain: Explorers sailed with maps that had blank edges and still crossed oceans. Inventors tried, failed, and tried again until something worked. Learn one name, one date, and one thing each person did. History sticks when it tells a story.
examples:
1492: Columbus sailed west across the Atlantic and reached the Americas.
Story to remember: three ships, a long voyage, a new map.
Explorers and inventors are both problem solvers: one crossed oceans, the other crossed the line of this does not work yet.
One name, one date, one result. Write the three in a row and say them once.

practice.question: In what year did Columbus sail across the Atlantic?
practice.hint: It is a 1400s date that starts with 149.
practice.praise: Yes! 1492 is the year.

practice.question: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
practice.hint: He stepped onto the Moon first, in 1969.
practice.praise: Correct! Neil Armstrong stepped out first.

practice.question: Why did explorers carry maps?
options: To find their way and show new places
practice.hint: Maps show where places are.
practice.praise: Right! Maps guided them and recorded what they found.

practice.question: An inventor who fails and tries again is...
practice.hint: Try, test, improve, repeat.
practice.praise: Nice! That cycle is the engineering process.

juniper_w4_m1.title: Regrouping: Add Six Numbers and Check by Estimating
juniper_w4_m1.summary: Add six numbers with regrouping in ones, tens and hundreds, then prove each sum by estimating first.
juniper_w4_m1.subject: math

content.explain: Regrouping is renaming: ten ones become one ten, ten tens become one hundred. Stack the numbers so the place columns line up, add one column at a time from the ones, and carry what you rename into the next column. The check that catches nearly every mistake is estimating: round each number to the nearest ten, add the rounded set, and see if your exact sum lands close. If it lands far away, you almost certainly dropped or double-counted a regrouped digit.

examples.q: Estimate first: 47 + 38 + 56
examples.a: 50 + 40 + 60 = 150, so an exact answer near 140–145 is sane.
steps: Round each to the nearest ten.

examples.q: Where do most errors hide?
examples.a: In the carried digit — written in the wrong column or added twice.

practice.hint: 7+8+6 = 21, carry 2 into the tens.

practice.question: Estimating helps because…
options: it catches sums that are far off
practice.hint: A sanity check on the exact work.
practice.praise: Right.

workbook.prompt: Add six two-digit numbers with regrouping, showing every step in a new colour.
workbook.answer: A correctly stacked sum with carry digits shown in a second colour.

workbook.prompt: Estimate that same sum first, then compare: how far off were you?
workbook.answer: An estimate and a difference statement.

workbook.prompt: Add six three-digit numbers with regrouping in ones, tens and hundreds.
workbook.answer: A correct three-digit sum with carries in the right columns.

workbook.prompt: Find and fix one deliberate error in a given sum; name the column it lived in.
workbook.answer: The corrected sum and the column named.

juniper_w4_rd1.title: Read It Twice: Sequence and Proof
juniper_w4_rd1.summary: First read for the story and the words you do not know; second read to put events in order and prove answers.
juniper_w4_rd1.subject: reading

content.explain: A story has a sequence even when it jumps in time: something happens first, then something forces a change, then the ending follows. Mark the events with numbers as you read — if the book flashes backward, number by story order, not page order. For every answer you give, you must be able to point at a line. That is the habit that makes comprehension reliable: claim then evidence, never a claim from memory alone.

examples.q: Page 4 begins with "That summer, before the fair…" — what number is it?
examples.a: It belongs early in the sequence, even though it appears later on the page.
steps: Place it on your event list.

examples.q: Question: Why did she go to the fair? What counts as proof?
examples.a: A line that states or strongly implies her reason — quoted with its line number.
steps: Write the line number beside the answer.

practice.question: Story order differs from page order when…
options: the book flashes back in time
practice.hint: Flashbacks break page order.
practice.praise: Yes.

practice.question: Proof for an answer is…
practice.hint: Point to the line that proves it.
practice.praise: Right.

workbook.prompt: Underline three words you do not know and write your guess from the sentence.
workbook.answer: Three underlined words with margin guesses.

workbook.prompt: Number the four main events of the passage in story order.
workbook.answer: Four events numbered 1–4 in story (not page) order.

workbook.prompt: Answer two questions and copy the proving line for each.
workbook.answer: Two answers each with a quoted proof line and line number.

workbook.prompt: Retell the passage in four sentences, then answer one why-question with evidence.
workbook.answer: A four-sentence retell plus an evidence-based why answer.

juniper_w4_sp1.title: R-Controlled Vowels: ar, or, ir
juniper_w4_sp1.summary: Sort the week’s words by ar, or and ir, then dictation: write all 10 from memory and fix misses.
juniper_w4_sp1.subject: spelling

content.explain: When an r sits right after a vowel, the vowel stops saying its usual name and they say one sound together: ar in car and hard, or in storm and short, ir in bird and first. That is why they are called r-controlled. Sort your list into three columns before you memorise anything — sorting by pattern beats sorting by alphabet, because your ear files the sound and your eye files the letters at the same time.

examples.q: storm — which column?
examples.a: or: the vowel+r says one sound, like in "or".
steps: Check for the r after it.
Say the sound, place the word.

examples.q: Why is "first" not spelled "ferst"?
examples.a: ir is the pattern for that sound in this word; er and ur carry it in others.
steps: Recall which pair appears in this word family.

practice.question: storm belongs to which group?
practice.hint: Vowel + r says one sound — "or".
practice.praise: Yes.

practice.question: In "hard", the ar sound is made by…
practice.hint: R controls the vowel.
practice.praise: Right.

workbook.prompt: Copy the 10 words once, syllable-marked, then sort them into ar / or / ir columns.
workbook.answer: Ten words copied and sorted into three columns.

workbook.prompt: Dictation: write all 10 from memory, then fix misses in a new colour.
workbook.answer: Ten dictated words with corrections in a second colour.

workbook.prompt: Write one sentence for each of three words you missed.
workbook.answer: Three sentences using the corrected words.

workbook.prompt: Cover, write and check the 5 hardest words, then re-test yourself once.
workbook.answer: A second clean pass on the five hardest words.

juniper_w4_gr1.title: Capital Letters, Commas and End Marks
juniper_w4_gr1.summary: Write four spelling words in sentences with capitals, one comma rule and the correct end mark.
juniper_w4_gr1.subject: english_grammar

content.explain: Three marks do most of the work in your writing. A capital letter starts a sentence and names a specific person or place. A comma separates items in a list and joins two complete sentences with a joining word (and, but, or). An end mark finishes the thought: period, question mark, or exclamation point. Read each sentence twice — once for meaning, once for marks — because your ear catches a missing comma that your eye skips.

examples.q: List: "We packed crayons, paper, and glue."
examples.a: Commas separate the three items; the last comma before "and" is optional but consistent.

examples.q: "The bell rang we ran" — fix it.
examples.a: Two complete sentences: "The bell rang, and we ran." (or a semicolon).
steps: Join with a comma plus a joining word.

practice.question: Which needs a comma? "We brought apples bananas and juice."
practice.hint: Items in a list are separated by commas.
practice.praise: Yes.

practice.question: Two complete sentences butted together need…
options: a comma plus a joining word
practice.hint: Join them properly or split them.
practice.praise: Right.

workbook.prompt: Write 4 sentences, one per spelling word; circle capitals, underline end marks.
workbook.answer: Four sentences with circled capitals and underlined end marks.

workbook.prompt: Write one three-item list sentence with correct commas.
workbook.answer: A list sentence with commas between items.

workbook.prompt: Repair a run-on: "The game ended we cheered."
workbook.answer: A fixed sentence joined with a comma and a joining word (or split in two).

workbook.prompt: Swap one period for a question mark and read it aloud to hear the change.
workbook.answer: A rewritten question with a question mark, read aloud.

juniper_w4_wr1.title: Order the Events, Then Write Them
juniper_w4_wr1.summary: Number the four story events in order, then write them as four sentences that read in sequence.
juniper_w4_wr1.subject: writing

content.explain: Before you write a retell, settle the order on scratch paper. Number the events 1 to 4 the way they happen in the story — not the way you remember them, the way the text proves them. Then write one sentence per event and lean on sequence words: first, next, after that, finally. Sequence words are the glue; without them, four correct events still read like four unrelated facts.

examples.q: Events: the ribbon was cut; crowds arrived; rides opened; prizes were judged.
examples.a: 1 crowds arrived → 2 rides opened → 3 prizes judged → 4 ribbon cut? Check the text — order must come from proof.
steps: Find the proving line for each order.

examples.q: "After that" — where does it go?
examples.a: Between sentence two and three, marking the move from one event to the next.
steps: Locate the two events it links.
Read aloud to check the flow.

practice.question: Which is a sequence word?
practice.hint: It marks order in time.
practice.praise: Yes.

practice.question: Events should be ordered by…
practice.hint: Evidence decides order.
practice.praise: Right.

workbook.prompt: Number the four events on scratch paper with a proving line for each.
workbook.answer: Four numbered events each backed by a line from the text.

workbook.prompt: Write the four sentences with sequence words at the joins.
workbook.answer: Four sentences linked by first / next / after that / finally.

workbook.prompt: Read aloud; mark any join where you stumbled and rewrite it.
workbook.answer: A revised version with smoother joins.

workbook.prompt: Check capitals and end marks, then copy the final clean version.
workbook.answer: A clean final copy with correct mechanics.

juniper_w4_lit1.title: Read a Chapter, Draw a Scene
juniper_w4_lit1.summary: Read a chapter, then draw one scene from it with a one-sentence caption.
juniper_w4_lit1.subject: literature

content.explain: A scene is one moment in one place: a slice, not the whole chapter. To choose it, ask which single moment changes something — a discovery, a choice, a reversal. When you draw it, include only what the text supports: if the author never described the weather, do not invent a storm. Your caption is the bridge between the picture and the book: one sentence that says what happens here and why it matters.

examples.q: Which moment to draw from a chapter about a lost book?
examples.a: The moment the name tag is found — it changes what the character will do.
steps: Pick the one that changes things.

examples.q: "Caption: Maya finds the name tag and realises whose book it is." — good?
examples.a: Yes: it names the moment and its consequence in one sentence.

practice.question: A scene is…
practice.hint: A slice of the story.
practice.praise: Yes.

practice.question: Your drawing should include…
practice.hint: Evidence-bound, like every retell.
practice.praise: Right.

workbook.prompt: List three candidate scenes from the chapter and circle the one that changes something.
workbook.answer: Three candidates with the pivotal one circled.

workbook.prompt: Draw the scene using only details the text supports; mark two text-backed details.
workbook.answer: A drawing with two annotated, text-backed details.

workbook.prompt: Write the one-sentence caption.
workbook.answer: A single sentence naming the moment and why it matters.

workbook.prompt: Write one question the scene raises for the next chapter.
workbook.answer: A follow-up question grounded in the scene.

juniper_w4_cv1.title: Jobs and Rules That Make a Community Work
juniper_w4_cv1.summary: Name four jobs or rules that make a community work and say why one of them matters most.
juniper_w4_cv1.subject: civics

content.explain: Communities run on a mix of people and rules. The jobs do the work; the rules make the work predictable — a stop sign means every driver does the same thing without negotiating each time. To judge which matters most, use one test: what breaks first if it disappears? Something that breaks many other things when it goes is load-bearing, like clean water rules or the people who enforce them.

examples.q: Four that make a community work: mail carrier, water inspector, crossing guard, library rule "return by the due date".
examples.a: Removing any one creates a specific, immediate problem for many people.
steps: Say what it prevents or delivers.

examples.q: Which breaks first if it disappears — the rule or the job?
examples.a: Often the rule first: without it the job still exists but cannot coordinate anyone.

practice.question: The disappearance test asks…
options: what breaks first if it is removed
practice.hint: Blast radius, not price.
practice.praise: Yes.

practice.question: Rules matter because they make…
practice.hint: Coordination without renegotiating each time.
practice.praise: Right.

workbook.prompt: Name 4 jobs or rules that make a community work and say why one matters.
workbook.answer: Four entries, each with a one-line reason.

workbook.prompt: Run the disappearance test on two of them; write what breaks first.
workbook.answer: Two absence scenarios with the first thing to break named.

workbook.prompt: Write one rule at home or school that works the same way.
workbook.answer: Analogous rule with its job named.

workbook.prompt: Draft one new job or rule your community needs and justify it with the test.
workbook.answer: A proposal plus a blast-radius justification.

test.title: Week 4 Test — Spiral review (Week 2 item set)
test.note: Drawn from Juniper's week-2 math lessons (times table review 2-5, equal groups & arrays, word problems with arrays, estimate to check) plus the daily spine practice activities. Spiral tier: this is the Week 2 item set reused for Week 4 until a Week 4 set is authored (G13 documented fallback). covers[] deliberately name the Week 2 lessons the items were written from.

questions.why: Zero groups of anything is nothing — you've got this!
Five groups of 3: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 — nice counting!

questions.q: Which shows 4 equal groups of 2?
questions.why: Four groups means four 2s added together — you spotted the pattern!

questions.q: An array has 3 rows and 4 columns. How many dots in all?
questions.why: Rows × columns: 3 × 4 = 12 — your array eyes are sharp!

questions.q: There are 4 bags. Each bag has 5 apples. How many apples in total?
questions.why: 4 groups of 5: draw 4 circles with 5 dots each, count them up — 20!

questions.q: A garden has 3 rows of flowers. Each row has 6 flowers. Which multiplication sentence matches?
questions.why: Rows × flowers in each row — you're reading the story like a math detective!

questions.q: Estimate first: 4 × 6 is about ?
questions.why: 4 × 6 is exactly 24 — your estimate was right on target!

questions.q: Which fact would you check by estimating 5 × 5 ≈ 25?
questions.why: Estimating 5 × 5 as 25 helps you know the answer makes sense — smart checking!

questions.q: Draw an array for 2 × 5. How many dots?
questions.why: 2 rows of 5 dots each — count by 5s: 5, 10. You've got array power!

questions.q: Complete the pattern: 2, 4, 6, 8, ___
questions.why: Counting by 2s — each step adds 2 more. You're cruising through the tables!

items.name: a dog
items.why: It eats, grows and breathes.

items.name: a rose bush
items.why: It grows and needs water and sunlight.

items.name: a mushroom
items.why: It grows and needs food to live.

items.name: a goldfish
items.why: It breathes, eats and grows.

items.name: a seedling

sets.title: Getting help when someone is hurt
Returning a library book
events: You put it in your bag
You hand it to the librarian
The librarian stamps the return card

sets.title: A crossing guard at the corner
events: The guard raises the stop sign

sets.title: The plumber fixes a leak
events: The plumber turns off the water

items.q: Which community helper puts out fires?
items.hint: Look for the helper with the bright red truck and the hose.

items.q: Who brings the mail to our street every day?
items.hint: This helper walks the same route after breakfast.

items.q: Who helps children cross the street at the corner?
items.hint: This helper carries a stop sign and wears a bright vest.

items.q: Who should you call if a pipe is leaking?
items.hint: This helper carries a wrench and fixes water pipes.

items.q: Where do you return a library book?
items.hint: This person works at the front desk of the library.

items.q: Who arrives in an ambulance when someone is hurt?
items.hint: This helper rides in the ambulance and knows first aid.

items.q: What does a crossing guard do first when buses arrive?
items.hint: The sign must go up before any child crosses.

items.q: Which helper do you ask when the toilet will not flush?
items.hint: This helper fixes water problems in a house.

items.q: Who checks the return bin at the library?
items.hint: She works beside the shelves and the stamp.

items.q: Why do community helpers practise their steps?
options: So they can use them without guessing
items.hint: The passage says helpers learn, practise, then use the steps.

items.question: Which block makes the sprite move forward?
items.hint: Sprites move when a MOVE block runs. The number tells how far.

items.question: A sprite has these blocks in order: say hello, move 5 steps, wait 2 seconds. Which runs FIRST?
items.hint: Blocks run from the top down, one after another.
items.praise: Yes - the top block runs first.

items.question: How many steps does this run?  move 5 steps, move 5 steps, move 5 steps
items.hint: Add the steps: 5 + 5 + 5.

items.question: You press run and nothing moves. What should you do FIRST?
options: Read the blocks from the top
items.hint: Debugging starts with reading the blocks, not guessing.
items.praise: Yes - read the blocks from the top.

items.question: Which block makes a sprite stand still for a moment?
items.hint: A WAIT block pauses the sprite without stopping the program.

items.question: Which of these is a BLOCK you could drag out?
items.hint: Blocks are short, exact instructions the computer understands.
items.praise: Yes - move 5 steps is a real block.

items.question: Change one block so the sprite moves 10 steps instead of 5. What do you change?
options: The number inside the move block
items.hint: The number inside a block is a value you can edit.

items.question: Your sprite moves forward but you wanted it to move back. Which block fits better?
items.hint: A negative number moves in the opposite direction.

items.question: Two blocks are in the wrong order: move 5 steps then say hello. You want the sprite to talk first. What do you do?
options: Drag say hello above move 5 steps
items.hint: Order matters: the top block always runs first.
items.praise: Yes - drag say hello to the top.

items.question: Which change makes the sprite do something NEW?
options: Add a turn block after the move
items.hint: A new block gives the sprite new behaviour.
items.praise: Yes - a turn block changes where it goes.

items.question: You add a wait block between two moves. What happens now?
options: The sprite pauses between the moves
The sprite moves twice as fast
items.hint: WAIT pauses the program at that point.
items.praise: Yes - it pauses between the moves.

items.question: You press run, then stop, then run again. Why does the sprite start from the beginning?
options: Run always starts at the first block
items.hint: Programs start at the top block every time you press run.
items.praise: Yes - run starts at the first block.

items.question: Which block would you add so the sprite moves 5 steps three times?
items.hint: A repeat block runs the blocks inside it again and again.

items.question: repeat 3 times wraps move 5 steps. How far does the sprite travel?
items.hint: The move block runs 3 times: 3 x 5 = 15.

items.question: Where do the blocks go that should be repeated?
items.hint: Only blocks inside the mouth of the repeat are repeated.

items.question: repeat 2 times: move 5 steps. How many steps in total?
items.hint: 2 x 5 = 10 steps.

items.question: What does the number inside repeat tell the sprite?
items.hint: That number is the number of times.
items.praise: Yes - how many times to repeat.

items.question: Which is the shorter way to move 5 steps four times?
items.hint: One repeat block replaces many copies.
items.praise: Yes - one repeat block does the job.

items.question: You wrote repeat 10 times but meant 3. What do you do?
options: Change the number inside repeat to 3
items.hint: The value inside the block is editable.

items.question: The sprite stops early. What is the BEST way to find the problem?
options: Read each block from the top and check it
items.hint: Debugging means reading carefully, not guessing.
items.praise: Yes - read the blocks from the top.

items.question: A pause block sits in the middle of your repeat. What should you do?
options: Move it out of the repeat if you did not mean to pause
items.hint: Unwanted pauses inside a loop slow everything down.
items.praise: Yes - move it out of the repeat.

items.question: Your program runs but the sprite goes the wrong way. What do you change?
options: The direction or sign in the move block
items.hint: Direction lives in the move value.

items.question: Which check happens BEFORE you press run?
options: Read the blocks in order and picture the result
items.hint: Good coders predict before they run.

items.question: You fix a block and run it again. Why?
items.hint: A fix is only a fix after you test it.
items.praise: Yes - run it again to prove the fix.

items.question: Your sprite moves 5 steps but should move 3. What is wrong?
options: The number in the move block
items.hint: The value inside the block is wrong.

items.question: Which sentence starts with a capital letter and ends correctly?
items.hint: A sentence starts with a capital and ends with a period.
items.praise: Yes - capital first word, period at the end.

items.question: Which sentence ends with a question mark?
items.hint: A question needs a question mark.

items.question: Which word must start with a capital letter?
items.hint: Names of people always start with a capital.

items.question: Which sentence is written correctly?
items.hint: Capital first letter, small letters after, period at the end.

items.question: Which sentence shows strong feeling with the right end mark?
items.hint: Strong feeling can end with a period or an exclamation point.

items.question: Which sentence is missing its end mark?
items.hint: Every sentence needs a mark at the very end.

items.question: Which sentence capitalizes the first word correctly?
items.hint: Only the first word and names need capitals here.
items.praise: Yes - My cat sleeps all day.

items.question: Which is a complete sentence?
items.hint: A complete sentence tells a whole idea and ends with a mark.

items.question: Which sentence ends with an exclamation point?
items.hint: Strong feeling or a warning ends with an exclamation point.

items.question: Which sentence uses capitals correctly?
items.hint: Days of the week always start with a capital.
items.praise: Yes - On Monday we baked bread.

items.question: Which sentence needs a question mark at the end?
items.hint: A sentence that asks something ends with a question mark.
items.praise: Yes - Do you want an apple?

items.question: Which word is NOT capitalized correctly?
items.hint: The first word of a sentence must be a capital.
items.praise: Yes - 'my friend Ava' should be 'My friend Ava'.

items.question: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
items.hint: It asks a question, so it needs a question mark.

items.question: Which title should start with a capital?
items.hint: Every important word in a title starts with a capital.
items.praise: Yes - My Trip to the Lake.

items.question: Which sentence ends correctly?
items.hint: A polite request is a statement and ends with a period.

items.question: Which sentence is written the BEST way?
items.hint: Capital first letter, normal letters after, period at the end.

items.question: Which sentence tells what happened FIRST in a story about a lost book?
options: Then I found it in the hall.
So I put it on the shelf.
items.hint: The first event comes before all the others.
items.praise: Yes - that is the first event.

items.question: Which sentence gives the clearest detail?
options: The dog ran across the yard.
items.hint: A strong sentence tells what and where.
items.praise: Yes - it names the action and the place.

items.question: Which order of three sentences retells a reading session?
options: First I read it. Then I answered. Last I checked.
Last I checked. First I read it. Then I answered.
Then I answered. Last I checked. First I read it.
items.hint: Order words first, then, last must match the events.
items.praise: Yes - the order words line up.

items.question: Which sentence is a complete thought?
items.hint: A complete sentence has a subject and a verb and ends with a mark.
items.praise: Yes - that is a complete sentence.

items.question: Which detail should NOT go in a retelling of the passage?
items.hint: Only details from the passage belong in a retelling.
items.praise: Yes - lunch is not in the story.

items.question: Which sentence retells the passage in order?
options: Maya lost the book, asked the librarian, then shared with Ben.
Ben lost the book, Maya hid it, the librarian left.
The librarian wrote a book, Ben read it, Maya went home.
Maya bought a book, Ben bought a book, they read.
items.hint: Follow the events exactly as the passage tells them.

items.question: Which word best starts a WHY sentence?
items.hint: A why sentence usually starts with because.

passages.title: A Story About a Lost Library Book
passages.text: Maya loved Tuesdays because that was library day. She always chose one big book and one funny book. One Tuesday the big book was missing from the shelf. Maya asked the librarian if anyone had returned it. The librarian checked the return bin and found the book under a stack of newspapers. A name tag inside the cover said it belonged to a second grader named Ben. Maya felt sorry that Ben had lost his book, so she gave it back to him and chose a different story. The next Tuesday Ben waved at her from across the reading room. Sharing the shelf made the whole room feel friendly.

passages.title: Community Helpers on Our Street
passages.text: Our street has helpers who work every day. The mail carrier walks the same route after breakfast. The crossing guard stands at the corner when the buses arrive. If a pipe bursts, the plumber brings tools to stop the water. If someone is hurt, a paramedic arrives in a bright red truck. Each helper follows steps that were taught to them. They learn the steps, they practise the steps, and then they use the steps. Knowing which helper does which job keeps our neighbourhood calm and safe.

passages.title: Living and Non-Living in the Garden
passages.text: In our garden a snail crawls over a wet stone. The snail is living because it eats, grows and moves on its own. The stone is not living, and it will never eat or grow. A fallen leaf was once living, but now it is dry and crumbly. Sunlight pours onto the plants and the plants drink it in. Rain is not living either, but living things could not survive without it. Look closely at any patch of ground and you will find both kinds of things side by side.

passages.title: The Sprite That Would Not Stop
passages.text: We built a sprite in the block editor and pressed run. The sprite moved five steps and waited for us. We added a repeat block so the sprite moved five steps three times. Then we pressed run again and the sprite ran across the whole screen. Our teacher asked us to find the one block that made it stop early. We read the blocks from the top, one at a time. The pause block was in the wrong place, so we moved it down. Debugging meant reading carefully, not guessing.

juniper_w5_l1.title: Mixed Facts and Fact Families
juniper_w5_l1.summary: Sort the x0-x9 facts you know from the ones you re-learn, then build two fact families.
juniper_w5_l1.subject: math

content.explain: A fact family is three numbers that belong together: 3, 4 and 12 give you 3 x 4 = 12, 4 x 3 = 12 and 12 / 4 = 3. Start by sorting your facts into two piles, know and re-learn. Work the re-learn pile with counters or an array so you can see the groups. Say the fact out loud before you write it, then cover the page and say it again from memory. Speed comes later; the pattern comes first.

steps: Check all three use the same three numbers.

examples.q: 6 x 7 gives 42. What else is true?
steps: Divide the product by one factor.

examples.q: You re-learned 8 x 7. How do you prove it?
examples.a: Draw 8 rows of 7, count the total, then say the family.

practice.question: Which fact family belongs to 5, 6 and 30?
practice.hint: A fact family uses one multiplication, its flip and one division.
practice.praise: Yes! Three numbers, three facts, one family.

practice.question: 9 x 6 = 54. Which division is in the same family?
practice.hint: Divide the product by one factor to get the other.
practice.praise: Yes! 54 shared into 6 groups leaves 9.

options: The one you must count on your fingers

practice.hint: The re-learn pile is for facts that are not automatic yet.
practice.praise: Yes! Re-learn means practise it again.

juniper_w5_l2.title: Weekly ELA: Animal Coverings
juniper_w5_l2.summary: Read the nonfiction page on animal coverings, then carry the same text into spelling, grammar and writing.
juniper_w5_l2.subject: reading

content.explain: Nonfiction writing has a main idea, and the other sentences are details that prove it. Read the page once for fun. Read it again with a pencil and underline the sentence that says what the whole paragraph is about. Then check each other sentence: does it prove that sentence, or does it just sit there? Details that do not attach get cut. The same text runs the whole week: you read it, spell from it, fix sentences from it and finally write from it.

steps: Find the sentence the others prove.

juniper_w5_l3.title: Habitats: Camouflage, Hibernation and Migration
juniper_w5_l3.summary: Three ways an animal survives when its habitat changes through the year.
juniper_w5_l3.subject: science

content.explain: A habitat has to supply food, water, shelter and space all year, and the year is not the same in every season. Animals answer the hard seasons in three main ways. Camouflage hides an animal from what is looking for it. Hibernation slows an animal right down so it needs almost no food. Migration is a long trip to somewhere warmer and better stocked. None of the three is smarter than the others; each one solves a different problem in a different place.

examples.q: A snowshoe hare turns white in winter. Which survival word is that?
examples.a: Camouflage.
steps: Ask what the change does for the animal.

examples.q: A ground squirrel sleeps through February. Which word?
examples.a: Hibernation.
steps: Notice the food is not there.

examples.q: Geese fly south each autumn. Which word?
examples.a: Migration.

practice.hint: Think about what winter removes from the habitat.
practice.praise: Yes! Slowing down stretches a thin food supply.

practice.hint: Migration involves travel.
practice.praise: Yes! The animal moves instead of waiting.

juniper_w5_l4.title: The People Who Built Our Town
juniper_w5_l4.summary: Put the jobs and events that made a town work into order on a timeline.
juniper_w5_l4.subject: history

content.explain: A town does not appear at once; it grows because people take on jobs. Someone surveys the land, someone builds the road, someone runs the store and someone teaches the children. Historians read those jobs the way you read a timeline: in order, and with a reason attached to each step. Ask two questions of every event. What changed because of it, and who benefited? Order first, meaning second. That is how a list of names turns into a story you can defend.

examples.q: A mill is built beside a river in 1840, and a village grows around it. What changed?
examples.a: Jobs and housing arrived, so families settled nearby.

examples.q: Why is the order of a timeline fixed?
examples.a: Nothing can be drawn to the left of something that happened later.

examples.q: Two sources disagree about a date. What do you do?

practice.hint: Think about what a river gives and what it carries.
practice.praise: Yes! A river is a pantry and a road at once.

practice.question: Who does a historian thank for a fact?
practice.hint: Every historical claim rests on a source.
practice.praise: Yes! Name the source and you can defend the claim.

workbook.answer: Four events in genuine chronological order, earliest left.

workbook.answer: A job paired with its consequence, e.g. builder -> road.

passages.title: Animal Coverings
passages.text: Every animal is dressed for its own weather. A polar bear has hollow hairs that trap warm air against its skin, and a layer of fat underneath holds the heat in. A desert beetle carries a bumpy shell that collects fog, so the water beads up and rolls straight to its mouth. A chameleon does not change colour to match the wall; it changes colour to show how it feels and how warm it is. A fish is covered in overlapping scales that lie flat and let it slip through the water. Coverings are not decoration. Feathers, fur, scales and shells each solve one problem: stay the right temperature, stay hidden, or stay moving.

juniper_w6_l1.title: Four-Digit Addition with Regrouping
juniper_w6_l1.summary: Add four-digit numbers in ones, tens, hundreds and thousands, showing every carry.
juniper_w6_l1.subject: math

content.explain: Regrouping is the same trick you learned with two digits, applied four times over. Start at the ones, add, write the digit and carry the ten. Move left to the tens, then the hundreds, then the thousands, and carry each time the column passes ten. Work right to left without skipping, because a carry changes the column on its left. When you finish, estimate first: round both numbers, add the rounded pair, and see whether your answer lands in the right neighbourhood.

steps: If it passes nine, you gain a digit.

juniper_w6_l3.title: Seasons and Weather Patterns
juniper_w6_l3.summary: Why the seasons repeat, and how a weather pattern differs from one day's weather.
juniper_w6_l3.subject: science

content.explain: Seasons come from the tilt of the Earth, not from how close the planet is to the Sun. In winter our half of the Earth leans away, so the light arrives at a shallow angle and spreads thin. In summer it leans toward the light and the same energy lands on a smaller patch. Weather is what is happening now; climate is the pattern of weather over years. That is why one cold week does not cancel a season, and why a pattern matters more than a single day.

steps: Each season follows the tilt around once.

examples.q: Weather or pattern: it rains most Tuesdays in April.

steps: Ask whether it repeats over years.
If yes, it is the pattern.

juniper_w6_l4.title: Early Explorers and Their Voyages
juniper_w6_l4.summary: Put the great voyages in order and name what each one changed.
juniper_w6_l4.subject: history

content.explain: Explorers sailed for trade routes, not for the sake of a new place. Columbus wanted a westward path to Asia and met two continents instead. Vasco da Gama went around Africa and reached India by sea. Magellan's crew completed the first circumnavigation, though Magellan himself did not. Read each voyage as a claim: who funded it, what they expected, and what actually happened. When the expectation and the outcome differ, that gap is where the history gets interesting.

passages.title: Ships That Carried Explorers
passages.text: Five hundred years ago a ship going west was a floating town. It carried barrels of water, salted meat, hard biscuit, rope, spare sailcloth and a cask of wine. Sailors slept on deck in foul weather and below deck in calm, in a space barely longer than a classroom. They navigated by the sun at noon and by the North Star at night, guessing their position rather than measuring it. Most voyages hugged the coast for weeks before striking out, because a coastline is a road that resupplies you. The ships were small, the oceans were not, and every landfall was a rumour until it was not.

juniper_w7_l1.title: Rounding to the Nearest 10
juniper_w7_l1.summary: Round two-digit numbers to the nearest ten, then use the rounded pair to estimate a sum.
juniper_w7_l1.subject: math

content.explain: Rounding asks which ten a number lives closer to. Look at the ones digit. Five or more rounds the tens digit up; four or less leaves it alone. A number line makes this visible: 47 sits between 40 and 50, closer to 50, so it rounds up. Estimating before you compute gives you a sanity check. If your exact answer and your estimate disagree wildly, one of them is wrong, and it is usually quicker to find out which by re-estimating than by re-adding.

Words like isobar and front are technical, so read the sentence around them before you reach for a glossary. Once the code is decoded, the map stops being a doodle and becomes an argument between air masses that you can follow.

juniper_w7_l3.title: Weather Tools and Forecasts

content.explain: Weather is measurement before it is prediction. A thermometer reads temperature, a rain gauge reads rainfall, a wind vane shows direction and an anemometer reads speed. A barometer reads pressure, and falling pressure is the classic hint that weather is about to turn. A forecast chains those measures into a claim about tomorrow, and a forecast is always a probability, never a promise. Read one with a question in mind: which measure supports it, and how confident is the wording?

passages.title: Reading a Weather Map
passages.text: A weather map looks like a doodle until you learn the code. A blue line with triangles is a cold front, and the triangles point the way it is moving. A red line with semicircles is a warm front. Where the two meet, air masses argue, and the argument is what we call weather. Numbers on the map are temperatures in the same units everywhere, so a cold 4 in the north and a mild 14 in the south tell one story. Isobars are the squiggly loops: when they crowd together the wind is brisk, and when they spread out the day is still. The map is a snapshot taken at one hour, so tomorrow it will have moved on.

juniper_w8_l1.title: Regrouped Addition and Missed Facts
juniper_w8_l1.summary: Re-teach the two weakest categories, then re-test cold with no practice first.
juniper_w8_l1.subject: math

content.explain: A checkpoint is not a punishment; it is a way of finding the exact hole so you can close it. Start by sorting your work from weeks one to seven into categories: facts, regrouped addition, word problems. Count the misses in each. Take the two worst categories and work four items each with a model beside you. Then stop practising and take ten cold items, because the only honest measure of a skill is what you can do before you warm up.

examples.q: You missed four facts and six regrouped sums. Where do you start?
examples.a: Regrouped sums, because that is the larger hole.

examples.q: Why test cold?
examples.a: Warming up hides which skills are actually secure.

examples.q: What counts as fixed?
examples.a: The same skill right twice, a day apart.

practice.question: Which is the fairest check of a skill?
options: Ten items with no practice first
Ten items after an hour of drilling
practice.hint: Cold testing hides nothing.
practice.praise: Yes! Cold items measure what is secure.

practice.hint: Ones 6+7=13 carry 1, tens 5+6+1=12 carry 1.
practice.praise: Yes! Two carries, one answer.

practice.question: A skill counts as fixed when...
options: you get it right twice a day apart
practice.hint: One success can be luck.
practice.praise: Yes! Spaced success is the honest bar.

workbook.prompt: Sort this week's misses into three categories and count them.
workbook.answer: Three labelled piles with a count in each.

workbook.prompt: Work four modelled items in your weakest category.
workbook.answer: Four items with the model shown beside each.

workbook.prompt: Take ten cold items and record the score.
workbook.answer: Ten items attempted without practice first, score recorded.

workbook.prompt: Name the one skill you will re-test tomorrow.
workbook.answer: One specific skill, not a subject name.

juniper_w8_l2.title: Weekly ELA: The Week the Reading Log Changed
juniper_w8_l2.summary: Read a narrative about a rule changing, then carry its vocabulary into spelling and writing.
juniper_w8_l2.subject: reading

content.explain: This passage reads like a story but argues like an essay, which is what a personal narrative does when it earns its point. Read it once for what happened. Read again and mark the moment the rule changed, then find the sentence that says why it mattered. Ask what the change cost, since every change costs something, and what it produced. Finally, use its words for spelling and write four sentences of your own about a rule you would change, with your reason attached.

examples.q: What was the old rule, and what replaced it?
examples.a: Title and page became one thing that happened.

examples.q: Why did the fake log become true?
examples.a: The new column asked for something the book had to supply.

examples.q: What is the last sentence doing?
examples.a: Generalising the small change into a claim about improvements.
steps: Read the claim built on it.

practice.question: The reading log improved because...
options: a student named the missing piece
practice.hint: Find who spoke up.
practice.praise: Yes! Ari named what the log never asked for.

practice.question: A personal narrative can also...
practice.hint: This piece tells a story to prove something.
practice.praise: Yes! Story in service of a claim.

practice.question: The phrase a margin means the change was...
options: small enough to fit beside the text
practice.hint: A margin is a narrow strip.
practice.praise: Yes! Small enough to write beside the column.

workbook.prompt: Write the old rule and the new rule in two lines.
workbook.answer: Two lines that show the before and the after.

workbook.prompt: Copy the sentence that states why the change mattered.
workbook.answer: The sentence linking the column to real sentences.

workbook.prompt: Use two words from this week's spelling list in one paragraph.
workbook.answer: A paragraph using both words with the right meaning.

workbook.prompt: Write four sentences about a rule you would change, with your reason.
workbook.answer: Four sentences: the rule, the change, the reason, the likely result.

juniper_w8_l3.title: Animal Groups Review
juniper_w8_l3.summary: Sort animals into groups by how they are born and what covers their bodies.
juniper_w8_l3.subject: science

content.explain: Scientists group animals by shared traits, and the two traits that do the most work are how young are born and what covers the body. Mammals have hair and feed milk. Birds have feathers and lay hard-shelled eggs. Reptiles have scales and mostly lay eggs on land. Fish have scales and gills and stay in water. Amphibians start in water with gills and later breathe air. A group is a hypothesis: if you find an animal that fits none of the five, the group list needs revisiting.

examples.q: A bat feeds milk and has hair. Which group?
examples.a: Mammal, even though it flies.

examples.q: A frog starts with gills and later breathes air.
examples.a: Amphibian.

examples.q: Why group at all?
examples.a: So a new animal's traits can be predicted from its group.

practice.question: Which animal is a mammal?
practice.hint: Hair and milk are the deciding traits.
practice.praise: Yes! Dolphins breathe air, have hair and feed milk.

practice.question: Feathers belong to which group?
practice.hint: Only one group has them.
practice.praise: Yes! Feathers are unique to birds.

practice.question: An amphibian typically...
options: starts in water with gills and later breathes air
practice.hint: Look for the change of breathing.
practice.praise: Yes! The switch from gills to lungs is the marker.

workbook.prompt: Sort eight animals into the five groups.
workbook.answer: Eight animals each placed in a defensible group.

workbook.prompt: Write the two deciding traits for each group.
workbook.answer: Body covering and how the young are born, for each group.

workbook.prompt: Draw one animal from each of three groups and label the trait.
workbook.answer: Three drawings with the matching trait labelled.

workbook.prompt: Explain to a parent why a bat is not a bird.
workbook.answer: Three sentences built on hair and milk rather than feathers.

juniper_w8_l4.title: Review: Helpers, Explorers and Our State
juniper_w8_l4.summary: Rebuild the quarter's timeline, name the sources, and fix anything that no longer holds.
juniper_w8_l4.subject: history

content.explain: A review is a reconstruction, not a re-read. Take a blank timeline and put the quarter's events on it from memory. Then open the lessons and check each placement. Anything you got wrong is the useful part of the exercise, because a corrected error sticks better than a rehearsed one. Finish by naming the source for three of the events. Facts you can source are facts you can defend; facts you only recall are facts you are renting.

examples.q: You place a voyage in the wrong decade. What now?
examples.a: Note the correction and why the mistake happened.

examples.q: What makes a source better?
examples.a: Closer to the event, dated, and checkable against another source.

examples.q: Name the three strands this quarter covered.
examples.a: Community helpers, explorers, and our state.

practice.question: The best first step in a review is...
options: rebuild it from memory, then check
practice.hint: Retrieval shows you the holes.
practice.praise: Yes! Memory first, notes second.

practice.question: Which source is strongest for a town's founding?
options: A dated council record from that year
practice.hint: Dated and close to the event wins.
practice.praise: Yes! Contemporaneous and checkable.

practice.question: Records of the past are kept so that...
options: we can trace how the town changed
practice.hint: Records are evidence of change.
practice.praise: Yes! That is history at town level.

workbook.answer: A first pass, a checked pass, and the corrections marked.

workbook.prompt: Name a source for three events and say why you trust each.
workbook.answer: Three sources with a stated reason for each.

workbook.prompt: Write one sentence for each of the three strands.
workbook.answer: Three sentences, one per strand, each accurate.

workbook.answer: One specific skill with a reason drawn from your own work.

passages.title: The Week the Reading Log Changed
passages.text: For six weeks our reading log had one rule: write the title and the page. Then Ari pointed out that the log never asked what the book was about, so half the class copied the title off the cover and guessed the rest. We added a single column called one thing that happened. The next week the log filled up with real sentences, and two people asked for books nobody had recommended. The change was small enough to fit in a margin. That is usually how improvements work: someone names the missing piece, the group writes it down, and the thing that was fake becomes true.

juniper_w9_l1.title: Mixed Facts, Sums and Word Problems
juniper_w9_l1.summary: Three categories in one sitting: facts, regrouped sums and word problems, sorted then re-learned.
juniper_w9_l1.subject: math

content.explain: Quarter review mixes skills on purpose, because real work never arrives sorted. Do the three categories in the order that costs you least: facts first while your head is fresh, then regrouped sums where careful column work matters, then word problems where you must first decide the operation. For a word problem, read it twice and underline the clue word before you compute. Finish by re-learning the two you missed, the same day, while the mistake is still specific.

examples.q: The clue word each makes shows which operation?
examples.a: Each and every often signal multiplication.

examples.q: You missed 9 x 7. What now?
examples.a: Draw 9 rows of 7, count it, say the fact twice.

examples.q: A word problem and a bare number ask for the same thing. What differs?
examples.a: The word problem asks you to choose the operation first.

practice.question: Each of 4 baskets holds 6 apples. How many apples?
practice.hint: Each signals equal groups.
practice.praise: Yes! Four equal groups of six.

practice.question: 7 x 8 = ?
practice.hint: Count by eights seven times.

practice.question: Which step comes first with a word problem?
options: Find the clue that names the operation
practice.hint: Choose before you compute.
practice.praise: Yes! The clue decides the operation.

workbook.answer: Eight items in three labelled piles.

workbook.answer: Three correct solutions, each with its clue underlined.

workbook.prompt: Re-learn the two facts you missed, with proof.
workbook.answer: An array, family or counter drawing for each missed fact.

workbook.prompt: Write one word problem of your own and swap it for a solution.

juniper_w9_l2.title: Weekly ELA: Mixed Passages, Mixed Questions
juniper_w9_l2.summary: Three short passages, three question types, one habit: point to the line that proves it.
juniper_w9_l2.subject: reading

content.explain: Mixed review asks you to switch modes, and switching is the skill. Passage one is informational, so look for structure. Passage two is literary, so look for character and motive. Passage three is practical, so look for directions. For every question do the same thing: answer in your head, then point to the line in the text that proves it. If you cannot point, you have guessed, and a guess that happens to be right is still a guess.

examples.q: A question about why a character acted looks for...
examples.a: Motive, found in what they said, wanted or feared.

examples.q: A question about a direction looks for...
examples.a: The exact step in the instructions.

examples.q: Your answer and the text disagree. What now?
examples.a: Trust the text and re-read the sentence you skipped.

practice.question: Proving an answer means...
options: pointing to the line in the text that supports it
practice.hint: Evidence is a line you can point to.
practice.praise: Yes! Point, then answer.

practice.question: In a literary passage, motive is...
practice.hint: Motive is the reason behind the action.
practice.praise: Yes! Say, want or fear gives the motive.

practice.question: In practical text you should read directions...
practice.hint: Instructions mean exactly what they say.
practice.praise: Yes! Literal reading is the right mode.

workbook.prompt: Label each of the three passages: informational, literary or practical.
workbook.answer: Three correct labels with one reason each.

workbook.prompt: Answer five questions and write the proving line beside each.
workbook.answer: Five answers each paired with a line from the text.

workbook.prompt: Copy one sentence you nearly got wrong and say why.
workbook.answer: The sentence plus the misreading that tripped you.

workbook.prompt: Write a main idea sentence for passage two.
workbook.answer: One sentence the details of passage two would prove.

juniper_w9_l3.title: The Science Fair: Choosing a Question
juniper_w9_l3.summary: Turn a curiosity into a question you can actually test with a fair comparison.
juniper_w9_l3.subject: science

content.explain: A science fair project lives or dies on the question. A good question names one thing you change, one thing you measure, and keeps everything else the same, because a fair test changes only one thing at a time. Which plant grows tallest is testable; which plant is nicest is not. Write your question first, then predict an answer with a reason, then design the comparison. If two things change at once and the result shifts, you will never know which change did it.

examples.q: Which plant grows tallest in one week is good because...
examples.a: One change, one measure, a fixed time.

examples.q: Which plant is the nicest fails because...
examples.a: Nicest cannot be measured the same way twice.

examples.q: Two things change at once. What do you do?
examples.a: Redo it with one change, or you cannot attribute the result.

practice.question: A fair test changes...
options: only one thing at a time
practice.hint: Otherwise you cannot say what caused what.
practice.praise: Yes! One change, one result.

practice.question: Which is a testable question?
options: Does more light make a bean plant taller?
practice.hint: Look for something you can measure.
practice.praise: Yes! Taller is measurable in centimetres.

practice.question: Your prediction should include...
practice.hint: A prediction is a claim plus why.
practice.praise: Yes! The reason is the science.

workbook.prompt: Write your testable question and name what changes and what you measure.
workbook.answer: One question with the changed variable and the measured variable named.

workbook.prompt: Write your prediction and the reason behind it.
workbook.answer: A prediction sentence plus a because.

workbook.prompt: List three things you will keep the same for every trial.
workbook.answer: Three controlled items held constant across trials.

workbook.prompt: Say how you will record the results.
workbook.answer: A table or graph plan with what each column holds.

juniper_w9_l4.title: Quarter 1 Review: Helpers, Explorers, Our State
juniper_w9_l4.summary: Rebuild the quarter on one timeline and defend three events with sources.
juniper_w9_l4.subject: history

content.explain: By now the quarter has three strands: the people who keep a town running, the voyages that reshaped the map, and our own state's story. Lay them on one timeline so the strands interleave instead of sitting in separate boxes. Then pick three events, one per strand, and defend each with a source. If two sources disagree, say so and say which you trust. Review is where you discover that a fact you recalled is not the same as a fact you can source.

examples.q: Why put all three strands on one timeline?
examples.a: So you can see what happened while other things were happening.
steps: Place all three strands on it.

examples.q: Two sources give different dates. What do you write?
examples.a: Both dates and which you trust, with your reason.

examples.q: What does our state's story add to the national one?
examples.a: Local detail: who settled where, and what the land allowed.
steps: Link it to the wider one.

practice.question: The strongest defence of a historical claim is...
options: a dated source you can point to
practice.hint: Evidence beats emphasis.
practice.praise: Yes! Date it and show it.

practice.question: Interleaving the strands on one timeline shows...
options: what happened at the same time as other events
practice.hint: One axis, several strands.
practice.praise: Yes! Contemporaneity is the payoff.

practice.question: Local history matters because...
options: it explains what the land and the people allowed
practice.hint: Think about place.
practice.praise: Yes! Geography shapes what a town can become.

workbook.prompt: Place nine events from the quarter on one timeline across three strands.
workbook.answer: Nine dated events, three per strand, correctly ordered.

workbook.prompt: Defend three events with a named source each.
workbook.answer: Three events, each with a source and a reason for trusting it.

workbook.prompt: Record one disagreement between sources and your judgement.
workbook.answer: Both claims plus which you trust and why.

workbook.prompt: Write one sentence linking our state's story to the national one.
workbook.answer: A sentence naming a real connection.

passages.title: Three Passages, One Habit
passages.text: Our review week used three short texts instead of one long one. The first explained how a bridge carries a load down its legs into the ground. The second told the story of a kid who returned a lost wallet and waited twenty minutes in the rain for its owner. The third gave the steps for making a paper aeroplane that actually flies. The questions changed each time, but the habit did not: answer, then point. Pointing is the difference between knowing something and hoping you do. Half the class discovered that the sentences they remembered best were the ones they had never actually read.

juniper_w10_l1.title: Division Facts as Sharing
juniper_w10_l1.summary: Split counters into equal groups, write the division, then flip it back into a family.
juniper_w10_l1.subject: math

content.explain: Division is sharing or grouping, and both readings are the same arithmetic seen from two sides. Share 24 counters into 4 piles and you get 6 in each. Ask how many piles of 4 you can make from 24 and you get 6 piles. Either way the answer is 6, and every division sits inside a fact family you already know: 4 x 6 = 24, 6 x 4 = 24, 24 / 4 = 6, 24 / 6 = 4. Draw it before you write it, because a picture catches a wrong answer faster than a second look.

examples.q: Share 24 counters into 4 equal groups.
examples.a: 6 in each group.
steps: Deal the counters round by round.

examples.q: Write the family for 6, 4 and 24.

examples.a: 7, because 5 x 7 = 35.

practice.question: 18 shared into 3 equal groups gives...
practice.hint: Ask how many in each pile.
practice.praise: Yes! Three piles of six make eighteen.

practice.question: Which division belongs to 8 x 5 = 40?
practice.hint: Dividing by one factor returns the other.
practice.praise: Yes! 40 shared into 5 groups gives 8.

practice.question: A remainder is...
options: what is left over after equal sharing
practice.hint: Equal sharing does not always use everything.
practice.praise: Yes! Leftovers are the remainder.

workbook.prompt: Draw 24 counters shared into 4 groups and label each group.
workbook.answer: Four groups of six, with the total marked.

workbook.prompt: Write the full fact family for 5, 7 and 35.
Solve six division facts and draw a picture for two of them.
workbook.answer: Six correct quotients with two supporting drawings.

workbook.prompt: Write one sharing word problem that has a remainder.
workbook.answer: A problem whose answer leaves a stated leftover.

juniper_w10_l2.title: Weekly ELA: Character Traits and Proof
juniper_w10_l2.summary: Read a story for how the character behaves, then carry the vocabulary into spelling and writing.
juniper_w10_l2.subject: reading

content.explain: A trait is not a feeling that passes; it is a pattern that repeats. To name one, gather two or three moments where the character does something similar without being told to. Then write the trait and the proof together, because a trait without evidence is just your opinion of somebody you have never met. Use the story's own words as your proof, quote a short line if it helps, and check that the line could not equally support the opposite trait.

examples.q: The character returns a wallet and waits twenty minutes in the rain. Trait?
examples.a: Honest, or conscientious.

examples.q: Could that line also prove the opposite trait?
examples.a: If yes, it is weak evidence; find a better line.
steps: Discard the line if it fits both.

examples.q: Is feeling scared a trait?
examples.a: Not by itself; everyone feels scared. What they do next is the trait.

options: a pattern of what they do
practice.hint: Look for repetition across the story.
practice.praise: Yes! Repeated behaviour is the evidence.

practice.question: Evidence for a trait should be...
options: a specific action or line from the story
practice.hint: Quote the text, not your feeling.
practice.praise: Yes! Specific and quotable.

practice.question: Which trait word fits a character who waits in the rain for a stranger?
practice.hint: They stuck to what was right.
practice.praise: Yes! Doing the right thing at a cost.

workbook.answer: A trait word plus two moments from the text.

workbook.prompt: Copy one line of dialogue that proves the trait.
workbook.answer: A short direct quote from the story.

workbook.prompt: Write four sentences: the trait, the proof, why it matters, and how it changes.
workbook.answer: Four sentences in that order, all text-based.

workbook.prompt: Argue the opposite trait using different evidence, then say which you accept.
workbook.answer: A counter-argument and a judgement with a reason.

juniper_w10_l3.title: Plant and Animal Life Cycles
juniper_w10_l3.summary: Compare four cycles side by side and name the stage each organism starts from.
juniper_w10_l3.subject: science

content.explain: Every life cycle is the same loop with different stations: birth or germination, growth, reproduction, and the next generation. A bean seed germinates in soil, grows roots and leaves, flowers, and drops new seeds. A butterfly hatches as a caterpillar, pupates, and emerges with wings. A frog starts in water with gills and later breathes air. Laying the cycles side by side shows what changes and what stays, and the question to ask at each stage is what this stage is for.

examples.q: What is a chrysalis for?
examples.a: Rebuilding the body from caterpillar into butterfly.

examples.q: Where does a bean cycle start?
examples.a: A seed in soil, with water and warmth.

examples.q: Why call it a cycle rather than a line?
examples.a: Because it returns to where it began.

practice.question: The correct order for a butterfly is...
practice.hint: Start with the egg.
practice.praise: Yes! Each stage sets up the next.

practice.question: A tadpole breathes with...
practice.hint: It lives in water first.
practice.praise: Yes! Gills in water, lungs on land.

practice.question: The purpose of a flower in a plant's cycle is...
options: to make seeds for the next generation
practice.hint: Think about what comes after the flower.
practice.praise: Yes! Fruit and seed follow the flower.

workbook.prompt: Draw four stages each for a bean and a butterfly.
workbook.answer: Eight labelled stages, correctly ordered.

workbook.prompt: Write what each stage is for in one sentence.
workbook.answer: One purpose sentence per stage.

workbook.prompt: Make a table comparing the plant and animal cycles.
workbook.answer: A two-column table of shared and differing stages.

workbook.prompt: Explain one difference between a frog cycle and a bird cycle.
workbook.answer: Three sentences naming gills versus hard-shelled eggs, accurately.

juniper_w10_l4.title: Inventors and Inventions
juniper_w10_l4.summary: Date the invention, name the need it answered, and read the notebook behind it.
juniper_w10_l4.subject: history

content.explain: Inventions are dated evidence: they tell you what a society could do and what it wanted done. Match each invention to the problem it answered, because inventions rarely appear from nowhere; they appear when an old answer stops being good enough. Then look for the notebook. The failures are the historical record, and a stack of dated mistakes usually explains a breakthrough better than a story about genius. Ask always who could afford the invention, since a thing only changes a country once people can get it.

examples.q: What does an invention date tell a historian?
examples.a: What a society could build and what it needed.

examples.q: Why value the failure notebook?
examples.a: It shows the thinking, not only the result.

examples.q: Why ask who could afford it?
examples.a: Because reach determines whether it changed anything.

practice.hint: Look for the failing predecessor.
practice.praise: Yes! Need pulls the invention into being.

practice.question: The failure notebook matters because it shows...
practice.hint: Process, not product.
practice.praise: Yes! It records what was tried and why.

passages.title: The Inventor Who Failed First
passages.text: The first version of the device did not work at all. Its inventor kept a notebook of every failure, dated and numbered, and the notebook is why we know his name. Failure one jammed because the seal leaked. Failure seven ran for four seconds and then overheated. Failure twelve worked, briefly, and told him what to fix next. Historians value that notebook more than the finished product, because the product shows what he made and the notebook shows what he thought. Progress is usually a stack of dated mistakes with one good result on top.

juniper_w11_l1.title: Four-Digit Place Value and Rounding
juniper_w11_l1.summary: Read and write four-digit numbers in every form, then round them to the nearest 100 and 1,000.
juniper_w11_l1.subject: math

content.explain: Place value is the address system of a number. In 4,726 the 4 is in the thousands column, the 7 in hundreds, the 2 in tens and the 6 in ones. Expanded form unpacks the address: 4,000 + 700 + 20 + 6. Rounding then asks which neighbour the number is closer to, whether the neighbour is a ten, a hundred or a thousand, and the rule is unchanged: five or more rounds up, four or less stays. Rounding is not losing precision on purpose; it is choosing the precision the question actually needs.

examples.q: Write 4,726 in expanded form.
Round 4,726 to the nearest hundred.
examples.a: 4,700, because the tens digit is 2.
steps: Two is less than five, stay.

examples.q: Compare 4,726 and 4,762.
examples.a: 4,726 is smaller; the tens column decides it.

practice.question: In 8,345 the digit 3 stands for...
practice.hint: Count the columns from the right.
practice.praise: Yes! The 3 sits in the hundreds column.

practice.question: Round 6,819 to the nearest ten.
practice.hint: The ones digit is 9.
practice.praise: Yes! Nine or more rounds the tens digit up.

practice.question: Which is the largest?
practice.hint: Compare hundreds first, then tens.
practice.praise: Yes! The hundreds column breaks the tie.

juniper_w11_l2.title: Weekly ELA: Maps and Legends
juniper_w11_l2.summary: Read a nonfiction page about maps for its text features, then spell and write from it.
juniper_w11_l2.subject: reading

content.explain: Nonfiction pages are built out of features that do real work. Headings sort the page into sections. Captions name and locate what a picture shows. A legend decodes symbols and a scale bar converts paper into ground. Read the headings first to get the shape of the piece, then the captions, then the paragraphs, because that order tells you what each block is for. When a caption and a paragraph disagree, the picture and the text are two sources, and you note the disagreement rather than picking quietly.

examples.q: Why read headings before paragraphs?
examples.a: They give the shape, so you know what each block is for.

examples.q: What does a legend do?
examples.a: Decodes the symbols so the map can be read.
steps: Look it up in the key.

examples.q: Caption and paragraph disagree. What now?
examples.a: Note both as sources and say which you trust.

practice.hint: It is a ratio between paper and ground.
practice.praise: Yes! Centimetres on paper become metres on the ground.

practice.hint: Everything else is a bearing from there.
practice.praise: Yes! North first, then bearings.

practice.question: Two sources disagree, so you...

practice.hint: Silent choosing is not history.
practice.praise: Yes! State the disagreement and your judgement.

workbook.answer: Four features, each paired with its job.

juniper_w11_l3.title: Earth's Surface: Land and Water
juniper_w11_l3.summary: Sort the surface into landforms and water bodies, then explain how each one changes.
juniper_w11_l3.subject: science

content.explain: The surface looks fixed and is not. Water, wind and ice wear rock away and carry the pieces somewhere else, which is erosion, and what they drop when they slow is sediment, which is deposition. A hill and a valley are both works in progress on a long clock. Rivers cut the outside of a bend and drop mud on the inside, so a meander walks across the floodplain over centuries. Learn the names of the shapes first, then ask what force shaped each one and how fast it is still working.

examples.q: What are the two great divisions of the surface?
examples.a: Land and water: continents and oceans.

examples.q: What does a river do on the outside of a bend?
examples.a: Cuts it, because the water is fastest there.

examples.q: What is sediment?
examples.a: The material dropped when water or wind slows.

options: wearing away and carrying off material
practice.hint: Think water, wind and ice at work.
practice.praise: Yes! Worn away and moved off.

practice.question: A delta forms where...
options: a river slows and drops sediment
practice.hint: Slow water drops its load.
practice.praise: Yes! Deposition at the river's mouth.

juniper_w11_l4.title: Geography and Maps of Our Country
juniper_w11_l4.summary: Read regions, borders and waterways, then explain why people settled where they did.
juniper_w11_l4.subject: history

content.explain: Geography is the stage the history stands on. Great Lakes waterways moved people and goods long before roads, a long growing season made the south farmable, and ice shaped which cities became ports. Read a map of the country first for physical features, then for borders, then for cities, and ask why each city sits where it does. Almost every answer is water, a crossing, a harbour or fertile ground. Once you can read the stage, the play stops looking random.

passages.title: Where Land Meets Water
passages.text: Stand at the edge of a lake and you are standing on a boundary that moves. Waves lift sand and drop it a few centimetres at a time, so a shoreline from a photograph taken fifty years ago rarely matches the one under your feet. Rivers do the same work faster, cutting a bend on one side and dropping the mud on the other. Ice is the slowest sculptor of all, but it grinds mountains into gravel given enough centuries. The surface of the Earth looks fixed from a classroom window, and it is not. Everything solid is just moving slowly enough to build a house on.

juniper_w12_l1.title: Unit Fractions and Comparing with Pictures
juniper_w12_l1.summary: Shade equal parts, name the unit fraction, and compare two fractions with a drawing.
juniper_w12_l1.subject: math

content.explain: A unit fraction names one part of something cut into equal parts: one half, one third, one fourth. The parts must be equal, or the fraction is a lie. The counter-intuitive rule is that a bigger bottom number makes smaller pieces, so one fourth is smaller than one third even though four is bigger than three. When you compare, draw both fractions the same size and shade them, because a picture settles the argument faster than an argument does.

examples.q: Shade one half of a bar split into two equal parts.
examples.a: One of two equal parts shaded, written 1/2.

examples.q: Which is bigger, 1/2 or 1/4?
examples.a: 1/2, because fewer parts means bigger pieces.

examples.q: Why must the parts be equal?
examples.a: Unequal parts make the bottom number meaningless.

practice.hint: One part out of four.
practice.praise: Yes! One of four equal parts.

practice.question: Which is larger, 1/3 or 1/5?
practice.hint: Fewer parts means bigger pieces.
practice.praise: Yes! Thirds are bigger than fifths.

practice.question: Fractions can only be compared when...
options: the wholes are the same size
practice.hint: Different wholes make comparison meaningless.
practice.praise: Yes! Same whole, then compare.

workbook.prompt: Shade and label one half, one third, one fourth and one sixth.
workbook.answer: Four correctly shaded shapes with unit-fraction labels.

workbook.prompt: Compare three pairs of unit fractions with a drawing.
workbook.answer: Three drawings with the larger fraction marked and justified.

workbook.answer: Four correct fractions.

juniper_w12_l2.title: Weekly ELA: Compare and Contrast
juniper_w12_l2.summary: Set two texts side by side, chart what they share and where they split, then write from the chart.
juniper_w12_l2.subject: reading

content.explain: Comparison runs on a chart with two columns and a shared topic at the top. List a feature down the middle, then record what each text says about it. Features that both fill are comparisons; features only one fills are contrasts. Signal words matter: and, also and both carry similarity, while however, unlike and on the other hand carry difference. Write your paragraph only after the chart is full, because a chart turns a vague impression into a claim you can support with a line from each text.

examples.a: The shared feature row, with a line quoted from each.

examples.q: One text blames flooding and the other blames drought.
examples.a: That is a contrast, with however as the connector.

examples.q: What if a feature only one text has?
examples.a: Still record it; an empty cell is information.

juniper_w12_l3.title: States of Matter
juniper_w12_l3.summary: Sort examples into solid, liquid and gas, then explain what changes between them.
juniper_w12_l3.subject: science

content.explain: The three states differ in how the particles sit and how freely they move. In a solid they are packed and hold their place, so the shape holds. In a liquid they slide over each other, so the shape follows the container. In a gas they fly apart, so the material fills whatever space it has. Heating adds movement and cooling removes it, and at each fixed temperature the material changes state rather than just getting warmer. That is why a pan of water stays at a hundred degrees while it boils.

examples.q: Water in a jug takes the jug's shape. State?
examples.a: Liquid.
steps: Does it hold its own shape?
No, so it is a liquid.

examples.q: Ice in the sun becomes water. Name the change.
examples.a: Melting: solid to liquid.

examples.q: Why does boiling water stop warming?
examples.a: The energy is going into changing state, not raising temperature.

practice.praise: Yes! It pours and reshapes.
