practice.hint: Skipping the liquid step entirely.
practice.praise: Yes! Frost forms this way.

practice.praise: Yes! Fixed positions, fixed shape.

juniper_w12_l4.title: Ancient Peoples and Rivers
juniper_w12_l4.summary: Follow two river civilizations and work out what the river made possible.
juniper_w12_l4.subject: history

content.explain: The first cities grew beside rivers for the same three reasons everywhere: water to drink, flat fertile soil that flooded on schedule, and a road for heavy goods. Farmers learned the flood calendar, surplus grain paid people to do other jobs, and bookkeeping arrived to track the surplus. Writing began as a receipt, not a poem. Follow one river from its banks to its mouth and you can watch a society move from farming to storage to records to government, in that order and for that reason.

examples.q: Why does surplus matter historically?
examples.a: It lets some people stop farming and specialise.
steps: Find the job it freed up.

examples.q: Why did writing appear first here?
examples.a: To record stored grain and trade.

examples.q: What does a flood calendar give a society?
examples.a: Predictable planting and irrigation.

practice.praise: Yes! Specialisation follows surplus.

passages.title: The Fraction of a Pizza Argument
passages.text: Two siblings argued about fairness for an entire afternoon. One had cut the pizza into eight slices and taken three. The other had cut an identical pizza into six slices and taken two, and insisted that three of eight was plainly more than two of six. Both were right about their own count and both were wrong about the comparison, because counting slices ignores the size of the slice. Line the slices up instead: three eighths of a whole covers less of the plate than two sixths of the same whole. The argument ended at dinner, and the rule that settled it was written on the fridge in marker.

pixel_w1_l1.title: Fraction Sense
pixel_w1_l1.summary: Numerators, denominators, and what the pieces really mean.
pixel_w1_l1.subject: math

content.explain: A fraction names part of a whole. The bottom number, the denominator, tells how many equal parts the whole is cut into. The top number, the numerator, tells how many of those parts you are counting. Neither number means anything if the pieces are not equal, so equal-sized parts come first.
examples:
A pizza cut into 8 equal slices with 3 eaten:
Denominator = 8 (total slices)
Numerator = 3 (slices gone)
Left = 8 - 3 = 5, so 5/8 remains.

2 of 6 tiles shaded:
2/6 of the shape is shaded.
The two numbers count different things: 2 shaded out of 6 total.
Reading 7/4 aloud: seven fourths. Because 7 is bigger than 4, it is more than one whole.

practice.question: A pizza is cut into 8 equal slices and 3 are eaten. What fraction is left?
practice.hint: Subtract the eaten slices from the total, then keep the denominator.
practice.praise: Correct! 8 - 3 = 5, so 5/8 is left.

practice.question: In the fraction 5/8, what does the 8 tell you?
options: How many equal parts the whole has
The total in a set of objects
practice.hint: The bottom number always counts the parts of the whole.
practice.praise: Right! The denominator 8 counts the equal parts.

practice.question: Four of ten equal parts are shaded. What fraction is shaded?
practice.hint: Shaded count on top, total parts on the bottom.
practice.praise: Yes! 4 shaded out of 10 is 4/10.

practice.question: In the fraction 7/4, which number is the numerator?
practice.hint: The numerator sits on top.
practice.praise: Exactly! The top number 7 is the numerator.

workbook.prompt: Write the fraction that shows 5 shaded parts out of 8.
workbook.answer: 5/8 - denominator is the total equal parts, numerator the shaded ones.

workbook.prompt: Name the numerator and denominator of 7/4 in words.
workbook.answer: Numerator 7 (parts counted), denominator 4 (equal parts in a whole).

pixel_w1_rd1.title: Who, What, Where on a Grade-5 Passage

Then read again hunting for the three question words: WHO is acting, WHAT happened, WHERE it took place. Each answer must point at a sentence you can underline. This week you record FIVE of them for the lab question, each with a unit - cm, mL, seconds, grams. If a sentence contains words like because or therefore, it has slipped into an inference; save that for the conclusion. The notebook is evidence, and evidence stays neutral.

pixel_w3_l2.summary: W1 D1 B6 - coding - Pixel grade 5

content.explain: W1 D1 B6 - coding - Pixel grade 5

Equivalent fractions name the same amount with different numbers. Multiply the top and the bottom by the same number and the value does not change, because you are really multiplying by one. You can divide the same way to reduce a fraction. This is why 1/2, 2/4, and 4/8 all land on the same point of a number line.
examples:
2/5 = ?/10:
The bottom doubled, so multiply the top by 2 too.
2 x 2 = 4
Answer: 4/10

9/12 reduced:
9 and 12 both divide by 3.
9 / 3 = 3, 12 / 3 = 4
Answer: 3/4
Check equivalence: 1/2 = 0.5 and 3/6 = 0.5, so they are equal.

practice.question: Which fraction is equal to 1/3?
practice.hint: Multiply the top and bottom by the same number: 1 x 2 and 3 x 2.
practice.praise: Correct! 1/3 = 2/6.

practice.question: Which fraction is equal to 2/5?
practice.hint: Double the top, so double the bottom.

practice.question: Fill in the blank: 3/4 = 9/ ?
practice.hint: The top was multiplied by 3, so do the same to the bottom.

practice.question: Which pair is NOT equivalent?
practice.hint: Turn both fractions into the same bottom number and compare.
practice.praise: Correct! 1/3 and 2/3 are different amounts.

workbook.prompt: Find the missing numerator: 2/5 = ?/10.
workbook.answer: 4/10 - the bottom doubled, so the top doubles.

workbook.prompt: Reduce 9/12 to lowest terms.
workbook.answer: 3/4 - divide top and bottom by 3.

workbook.prompt: Write two fractions equal to 1/2.
workbook.answer: 2/4, 4/8, 3/6 or 5/10 - any equivalent pair.

workbook.prompt: Explain why 3/6 = 1/2 without using decimals.
workbook.answer: Both name the same amount: 3 of 6 equal parts is half of the whole.

pixel_w1_rd2.title: Main Idea and Two Details
pixel_w1_rd2.summary: Underline the sentence that states the main idea and note two supporting details.
pixel_w1_rd2.subject: reading

content.explain: The main idea is the sentence the rest of the paragraph is there to support. A reliable test: after reading a paragraph, ask what single sentence would still make the paragraph useful if everything else were cut. That sentence is usually the topic sentence - often first, sometimes last. Two supporting details then prove it: each must attach to the main idea, not merely appear in the paragraph.

examples.q:
Paragraph about fair tests. Main idea: 'A fair test changes only one thing at a time.'
Detail: 'If two things change you cannot tell which one mattered.'
examples.a: Detail supports the main idea.
steps: Check every other sentence attaches to it.

examples.q: Detail: 'The lab notebook was blue.' Does it support the main idea?
examples.a: No - it is incidental, not evidence.

examples.q: Main idea stated last: 'Cooking is one of the few places where an improper fraction appears on a Tuesday morning.'
examples.a: Topic sentences sometimes close a paragraph.

workbook.answer: One sentence that the whole paragraph supports.

workbook.answer: Two details, each with a phrase naming the link to the main idea.

workbook.answer: One discarded detail with a reason.

pixel_w1_cod2.title: Build the Program from the Checklist
pixel_w1_cod2.summary: Write the print(), variables and indentation program from the checklist and run it twice.

The checklist for this week: a print() with quotes, a variable assigned with a single equals sign, a line that updates that variable, and an indented block that belongs to a condition. Type it, read it aloud, run it. Then run it a second time - a program that behaves the same way twice is a program you understand rather than one you got lucky with.

pixel_w1_l3.title: Area & Perimeter
pixel_w1_l3.summary: Walk the edge for perimeter; fill the inside for area.
pixel_w1_l3.subject: math

content.explain: Perimeter is the distance around a shape, so you add every side as you walk the edge. Area is the space inside, measured in square units, and for a rectangle it is length times width. An 8-by-5 rectangle has a perimeter of 26 units and an area of 40 square units. Never mix the units: perimeter uses units, area uses square units.
examples:
Rectangle 8 by 5:
Perimeter = 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26 units
Area = 8 x 5 = 40 square units

Rectangle 7 by 3:
Perimeter = 7 + 3 + 7 + 3 = 20 units
Area = 7 x 3 = 21 square units

Square with side 6:
Perimeter = 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 24 units
Area = 6 x 6 = 36 square units

practice.question: A rectangle is 8 by 5. What is its area?
practice.hint: Area of a rectangle is length times width.
practice.praise: Yes! 8 x 5 = 40 square units.

practice.question: A rectangle is 8 by 5. What is its perimeter?
practice.hint: Add all four sides: 8 + 5 + 8 + 5.
practice.praise: Correct! The perimeter is 26 units.

practice.question: A rectangle has an area of 21 and one side of 7. How long is the other side?
practice.hint: Divide the area by the side you know: 21 / 7.

practice.question: A square has sides of 6. What is its perimeter?
practice.hint: A square has four equal sides, so add 6 four times.
practice.praise: Exactly! 6 x 4 = 24 units.

workbook.prompt: A rectangle is 8 by 5. Find area and perimeter.
workbook.answer: Area 40 square units; perimeter 26 units.

workbook.prompt: A square has a side of 6. Find area and perimeter.
workbook.answer: Area 36 square units; perimeter 24 units.

workbook.prompt: Area is 45 and width is 5. Find the length.
workbook.answer: 9 units - 45 divided by 5.

workbook.prompt: Explain why perimeter and area never share units.
workbook.answer: Perimeter counts length units along the edge; area counts square units inside.

workbook.answer: A clean second sort with all five placed correctly.

pixel_w1_sci4.title: The Mini Lab Report
pixel_w1_sci4.summary: Question, method, result - written properly, then take the weekly test.
pixel_w1_sci4.subject: science

content.explain: A mini lab report is three short sections in a fixed order. QUESTION states what you set out to find, written so it could be answered with data. METHOD lists what you changed, what you measured and how many trials you ran - enough that a classmate could repeat it. RESULT gives the numbers and the pattern without explaining them yet. Keep the sections separate; a report that mixes them is the most common reason a lab note loses marks.

examples.q:
QUESTION: Does the amount of water change how long dissolving takes?
METHOD: Same solid, three volumes, three trials each.
RESULT: 50 mL = 14 s, 100 mL = 11 s, 150 mL = 9 s.
examples.a: Three sections, result free of explanation.

examples.q: METHOD: 'We did it and it was quick.'
examples.a: Not repeatable - add volumes, masses and trial counts.

examples.q: RESULT: 'Water makes it dissolve faster.'
examples.a: That is the conclusion, not the result. Move it.
steps: Move the claim to the conclusion.

workbook.prompt: Write the QUESTION section.
workbook.answer: One testable question written to be answered with numbers.

workbook.prompt: Write the METHOD section.
workbook.answer: Changed variable, measured variable and trial count, in enough detail to repeat.

workbook.prompt: Write the RESULT section with the actual numbers.
workbook.answer: Numbers plus the observed pattern, with no explanation.

workbook.prompt: Read the three sections back and confirm they stay separate.
workbook.answer: A separation check - no conclusions inside the result.

pixel_w1_hist4.title: Retell Map Skills in Four Sentences
pixel_w1_hist4.summary: Retell equator, hemispheres and continents in four sentences: who, when, where, why.
pixel_w1_hist4.subject: history

content.explain: A four-sentence retell uses the four question words on purpose: WHO used the idea and when, WHERE it applies on the globe, and WHY anyone should care. Write them in that order and keep each sentence doing one job. The test of the retell is that a listener who has never read the source can repeat the idea back correctly after hearing your four sentences.

examples.q: S1: navigators in the 1800s used the equator as a reference. S2: They fixed it at the widest part of the globe. S3: It splits Earth into two hemispheres. S4: It mattered because latitude could be measured at sea.
examples.a: Who, when, where, why - one job each.

examples.q: S3 repeats S1 in different words.
examples.a: Cut the echo and give 'where' its own content.

examples.q: S4: 'It was important.'
examples.a: Why important? Name the measurement.

workbook.prompt: Write sentence 1: who used this idea and when.
workbook.answer: One sentence naming people and a period.

workbook.prompt: Write sentence 2: where it applies on the globe.
workbook.answer: One sentence locating the feature on Earth.

workbook.prompt: Write sentence 3: what it divides the Earth into.
workbook.answer: One sentence naming the hemispheres.

workbook.prompt: Write sentence 4: why it mattered.
workbook.answer: One sentence naming the practical reason, not 'it was important'.

pixel_w1_cod4.title: Add One New Feature
pixel_w1_cod4.summary: Extend the program with one new feature, then take the weekly test.
pixel_w1_cod4.subject: coding

content.explain: Extending a working program is the safest way to learn: keep the part that runs, add one feature, run again. Good first features for this program are a loop that repeats the print, an input() that asks for a name, or a second variable used in the output. One feature at a time. If the program breaks, remove the feature, confirm the original still runs, then add it back with a change.

examples.q: Add: for i in range(3): print("Hello")
examples.a: The greeting now prints three times.
steps: Add it below the working code.

examples.q: Add: name = input("Name: ") then print(name)
examples.a: The program now asks for and echoes a name.

examples.q: After adding two features the program fails.
examples.a: Revert to the working version, then add ONE at a time.

workbook.prompt: Choose one new feature and write down what it will do.
workbook.answer: A one-line feature plan in plain language.

workbook.prompt: Add the feature to your program.
workbook.answer: The new line or block inserted below the working code.

workbook.prompt: Run it and confirm the feature works.
workbook.answer: A run showing the new behaviour.

workbook.prompt: Run it once more and write one sentence on what you would add next.
workbook.answer: A second confirming run plus one honest next-step sentence.

questions.q: A pizza is cut into 8 equal slices and 3 are eaten. What fraction is left?
questions.why: 8 slices minus 3 eaten = 5 left out of 8, and the bottom number stays 8: 5/8.

questions.q: In the fraction 5/8, what does the 8 tell you?
options: How many equal parts the whole has
questions.why: The denominator (bottom) always counts the equal parts of the whole, not the part you hold.

questions.q: Four of ten equal parts are shaded. Which fraction shows the shaded part?
questions.why: Shaded count goes on top, total equal parts on the bottom.

questions.q: In the fraction 7/4, which number is the numerator?
questions.why: The numerator is the top number; because 7 is bigger than 4, this fraction is more than one whole.

questions.q: Which fraction is equal to 1/3?
questions.why: Multiply top AND bottom by the same number: 1 x 2 = 2 and 3 x 2 = 6, so 2/6.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: 3/4 = 9/ ?
questions.why: The top was multiplied by 3, so multiply the bottom by 3 too: 4 x 3 = 12.

questions.q: Which pair is NOT equivalent?
questions.why: Same bottom, different tops: 2/3 is twice as much as 1/3, so they name different amounts.

questions.q: What is 2/3 of 18?
questions.why: Split 18 into 3 equal parts (6 each), then take 2 of those parts: 6 x 2 = 12.

questions.q: A rectangle is 9 by 4. What is its perimeter?
questions.why: Perimeter adds the four sides: 9 + 4 + 9 + 4 = 26. The 36 is the AREA, not the perimeter.

questions.q: Which line stores the number 7 in a variable called score?
questions.why: A single equals sign stores a value, and the variable name goes on the left.

questions.q: Which line correctly prints Hello in Python?
questions.why: Text needs quotes so Python knows it is a word to show, and printing needs parentheses.

questions.q: What is wrong with the line:  print Hello
questions.why: Python must be told which part is text (quotes) and how to show it — print( ).

questions.q: In Python, text such as "cat" is called a...
questions.why: A string is a sequence of characters; numbers like 7 need no quotes.

questions.q: Which word is spelled correctly?
questions.why: Picture a rat running through the middle: sep-a-rat-e.

passages.title: The Line Around the Middle
passages.text: Cartographers draw an imaginary line around the widest part of the Earth and call it the equator. Because the planet is a sphere, that line splits it into a Northern Hemisphere and a Southern Hemisphere. Countries near the equator receive nearly the same amount of sunlight all year, so their seasons look nothing like ours. Sailors once used the line on their charts to keep track of latitude, and a navigator could tell how far north or south a ship had travelled by measuring the height of the sun at noon. The line is imaginary, but the differences it describes are real.

passages.title: One Fair Question
passages.text: A fair test begins with one question that can be answered with numbers. First you write a hypothesis, which is a prediction you could prove wrong. Then you list the steps, choose what you will change, and decide what you will measure. Only one thing changes in a fair test, because if two things change you can never tell which one caused the result. Observations go into the lab notebook as you work, with units beside every number. When the data is complete, you look for a pattern before you write the conclusion. A conclusion that ignores the data is only a story.

passages.title: Sailing by the Stars
passages.text: Long before satellites, navigators crossed oceans using a compass and a table of stars. Vasco da Gama rounded the tip of Africa and reached India by sea in 1498, following a route that European ships had never sailed. Twenty years later Magellan's expedition set out to circle the whole world, and one ship completed the journey. These voyages changed the maps that people kept at home, because lands that had been drawn as guesses became coastlines with names. Exploration also brought conquest and disease, which is why a modern history book tells the voyages from more than one side.

passages.title: Fractions at the Counter
passages.text: A recipe for granola calls for three quarters of a cup of oats and half a cup of nuts. If you double the recipe, you multiply every fraction by two: three quarters becomes six quarters, which is one whole cup and a half. Cooking is one of the few places where an improper fraction appears on a Tuesday morning, and nobody stops to worry about it. The denominator never changes its job, because it still tells you how many equal parts make a whole. Measure carefully, keep the units straight, and the batch will come out the same way twice.

test.note: Drawn from Pixel's mapped week-2 lessons: volume, solving for x, variables, equations, plus fraction operations and cross-curricular practice. covers[] rebound to the in-week lessons of the subjects the items ask about (math, sentence structure, spelling, properties of matter, ancient civilizations); the two volume items preview the Week 4 unit. questions.q: A box is 4 cm long, 3 cm wide, and 2 cm high. What is its volume in cubic centimeters?
questions.why: Volume = length × width × height = 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 cubic cm. Great job visualizing the unit cubes!

questions.q: If you fill a box with 36 unit cubes and the box is 3 cubes long and 4 cubes wide, how many layers high is it?
questions.why: Each layer has 3 × 4 = 12 cubes. 36 ÷ 12 = 3 layers. You're thinking in 3D!

questions.q: Solve for x: x + 7 = 15
questions.why: Undo the +7 by subtracting 7 from both sides: x = 15 - 7 = 8. Nice inverse thinking!

questions.q: Solve for x: 3x = 21
questions.why: Undo the multiplication by dividing both sides by 3: x = 21 ÷ 3 = 7. You've got the balance scale idea!

questions.q: In the expression 5 + n = 12, what does the letter n represent?
options: An unknown number we need to find
questions.why: A variable like n is a placeholder for a number we don't know yet. It's a math detective's clue!

questions.q: Which equation shows the rule: 'Multiply a number by 4, then add 3'?
questions.why: The rule says multiply first (4x), then add 3. That's exactly y = 4x + 3. You're reading math like a story!

questions.q: What is 3/8 + 2/8?
questions.why: Same denominator means same-sized pieces: 3 pieces + 2 pieces = 5 pieces out of 8. Smooth sailing!
Keep the denominator, subtract the numerators: 7 - 3 = 4, so 4/10. You're keeping the whole intact!

questions.q: What is 2/5 of 20?
questions.why: Split 20 into 5 equal groups (4 each), take 2 groups: 4 × 2 = 8. Fraction of a quantity mastered!

questions.q: In the sentence 'The curious robot explored Mars', what is the complete subject?
questions.why: The complete subject includes all the words telling who or what: 'The curious robot'. You spotted the whole team!

questions.q: Which of these is a sentence fragment?
options: The sun rises in the east.
questions.why: 'Because it was raining' leaves you waiting for the rest of the thought. It's a dependent clause, not a complete sentence. Sharp eye!

questions.q: When adding -ing to 'run', what spelling rule applies?
questions.why: Run has a short vowel + one consonant, so double the n: running. You've got the doubling rhythm down!

questions.q: Which property helps you identify a solid?
options: Takes the shape of its container
Has a definite shape and volume
questions.why: Solids keep their own shape and volume. That's why a rock stays a rock wherever you put it. Solid reasoning!

questions.q: Why did ancient cities often grow near rivers?
options: For water, farming, travel, and trade
questions.why: Rivers gave fresh water, fertile soil for crops, transportation, and trade routes — everything a city needs to thrive. You're thinking like a historian!

passages.title: The Line Around the Middle
passages.text: Cartographers draw an imaginary line around the widest part of the Earth and call it the equator. Because the planet is a sphere, that line splits it into a Northern Hemisphere and a Southern Hemisphere. Countries near the equator receive nearly the same amount of sunlight all year, so their seasons look nothing like ours. Sailors once used the line on their charts to keep track of latitude, and a navigator could tell how far north or south a ship had travelled by measuring the height of the sun at noon. The line is imaginary, but the differences it describes are real.

passages.title: One Fair Question
passages.text: A fair test begins with one question that can be answered with numbers. First you write a hypothesis, which is a prediction you could prove wrong. Then you list the steps, choose what you will change, and decide what you will measure. Only one thing changes in a fair test, because if two things change you can never tell which one caused the result. Observations go into the lab notebook as you work, with units beside every number. When the data is complete, you look for a pattern before you write the conclusion. A conclusion that ignores the data is only a story.

passages.title: Sailing by the Stars
passages.text: Long before satellites, navigators crossed oceans using a compass and a table of stars. Vasco da Gama rounded the tip of Africa and reached India by sea in 1498, following a route that European ships had never sailed. Twenty years later Magellan's expedition set out to circle the whole world, and one ship completed the journey. These voyages changed the maps that people kept at home, because lands that had been drawn as guesses became coastlines with names. Exploration also brought conquest and disease, which is why a modern history book tells the voyages from more than one side.

passages.title: Fractions at the Counter
passages.text: A recipe for granola calls for three quarters of a cup of oats and half a cup of nuts. If you double the recipe, you multiply every fraction by two: three quarters becomes six quarters, which is one whole cup and a half. Cooking is one of the few places where an improper fraction appears on a Tuesday morning, and nobody stops to worry about it. The denominator never changes its job, because it still tells you how many equal parts make a whole. Measure carefully, keep the units straight, and the batch will come out the same way twice.

pixel_w3_l4.title: Make a Tiny Page
pixel_w3_l4.summary: Put headings and paragraphs together into one small page.
pixel_w3_l4.subject: coding

content.explain: A whole page follows one skeleton: doctype, html, head, then body. The head stores page settings, while the body holds everything a person can see. Inside the body, headings introduce sections and paragraphs carry the text. Build the smallest page that works first, then add to it, because four correct lines already render.
examples:
Camp Notes

Day one: we saw a hawk.
Order matters: <!DOCTYPE html> first, then <html>, then <body>, and every tag you open gets closed.
Save as index.html and open it in a browser: even four lines render a real page.

practice.question: Which line comes first in an HTML page?
practice.hint: The doctype tells the browser which version of HTML to expect.
practice.praise: Correct! <!DOCTYPE html> goes on the very first line.

practice.question: Where does the content a person can see go?
practice.hint: The head is for settings; the other is for the page itself.
practice.praise: Yes! Everything visible lives in <body>.

practice.question: Which shows a heading followed by a paragraph?
practice.hint: An h1 is the heading and a p is the paragraph, each closed properly.
practice.praise: Right! h1 first, then a closed p.

practice.question: In <title>Camp</title>, where does Camp show up?
practice.hint: The title is page metadata, not body content.
practice.praise: Exactly! The title appears in the browser tab.

questions.q: A box is 4 cm long, 3 cm wide, and 2 cm high. What is its volume in cubic centimeters?
questions.why: Volume = length × width × height = 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 cubic cm. Great job visualizing the unit cubes!

questions.q: If you fill a box with 36 unit cubes and the box is 3 cubes long and 4 cubes wide, how many layers high is it?
questions.why: Each layer has 3 × 4 = 12 cubes. 36 ÷ 12 = 3 layers. You're thinking in 3D!

questions.q: Solve for x: x + 7 = 15
questions.why: Undo the +7 by subtracting 7 from both sides: x = 15 - 7 = 8. Nice inverse thinking!

questions.q: Solve for x: 3x = 21
questions.why: Undo the multiplication by dividing both sides by 3: x = 21 ÷ 3 = 7. You've got the balance scale idea!

questions.q: In the expression 5 + n = 12, what does the letter n represent?
options: An unknown number we need to find
questions.why: A variable like n is a placeholder for a number we don't know yet. It's a math detective's clue!

questions.q: Which equation shows the rule: 'Multiply a number by 4, then add 3'?

passages.title: The Line Around the Middle
passages.text: Cartographers draw an imaginary line around the widest part of the Earth and call it the equator. Because the planet is a sphere, that line splits it into a Northern Hemisphere and a Southern Hemisphere. Countries near the equator receive nearly the same amount of sunlight all year, so their seasons look nothing like ours. Sailors once used the line on their charts to keep track of latitude, and a navigator could tell how far north or south a ship had travelled by measuring the height of the sun at noon. The line is imaginary, but the differences it describes are real.

passages.title: One Fair Question
passages.text: A fair test begins with one question that can be answered with numbers. First you write a hypothesis, which is a prediction you could prove wrong. Then you list the steps, choose what you will change, and decide what you will measure. Only one thing changes in a fair test, because if two things change you can never tell which one caused the result. Observations go into the lab notebook as you work, with units beside every number. When the data is complete, you look for a pattern before you write the conclusion. A conclusion that ignores the data is only a story.

passages.title: Sailing by the Stars
passages.text: Long before satellites, navigators crossed oceans using a compass and a table of stars. Vasco da Gama rounded the tip of Africa and reached India by sea in 1498, following a route that European ships had never sailed. Twenty years later Magellan's expedition set out to circle the whole world, and one ship completed the journey. These voyages changed the maps that people kept at home, because lands that had been drawn as guesses became coastlines with names. Exploration also brought conquest and disease, which is why a modern history book tells the voyages from more than one side.

passages.title: Fractions at the Counter
passages.text: A recipe for granola calls for three quarters of a cup of oats and half a cup of nuts. If you double the recipe, you multiply every fraction by two: three quarters becomes six quarters, which is one whole cup and a half. Cooking is one of the few places where an improper fraction appears on a Tuesday morning, and nobody stops to worry about it. The denominator never changes its job, because it still tells you how many equal parts make a whole. Measure carefully, keep the units straight, and the batch will come out the same way twice.

pixel_w4_l3.title: Explorers & Discovery
pixel_w4_l3.summary: Voyages, maps, and the age of exploration.
pixel_w4_l3.subject: history

content.explain: The Age of Exploration ran roughly from the 1400s to the 1600s, when European ships reached Asia, Africa, and the Americas by sea. Better compasses, sturdier ships, and the search for new trade routes pushed the voyages forward. Exploration brought new exchange of goods and ideas, and also conquest and disease, so both halves belong in the story. Learn each explorer with a year, a route, and a result.
examples:
1492 - Columbus: sailed west from Spain and reached the Caribbean.
1498 - Vasco da Gama: reached India by sea, around Africa.
1519-1522 - Magellan's expedition: first to sail all the way around the world.
Route map: da Gama = India, Columbus = Americas, Magellan = around the world.
Year, route, result. Three beats per explorer keeps the memory solid.

pixel_w4_l4.title: Mixed Language Review
pixel_w4_l4.summary: Pull punctuation, spelling, and reading together.
pixel_w4_l4.subject: reading

content.explain: Mixed review pulls punctuation, spelling, and reading into one pass, exactly the way the quiz will. Read the whole sentence before you look at the options. Then ask three things: does it end correctly, is each word spelled correctly, and does the meaning still hold. One careful re-read catches most mistakes.
examples:
Read: The crew set sail in 1498, then anchored near India.
Punctuation: comma after the year, period at the end.
Spelling: anchored and sail are both correct.
Question tools on that sentence: who (the crew), when (1498), where (near India), why (the trade voyage).
Spelling sweep: check the middle of each word first, because the ends are usually easy.

questions.q: A box is 4 cm long, 3 cm wide, and 2 cm high. What is its volume in cubic centimeters?

questions.why: Each layer has 3 × 4 = 12 cubes. 36 ÷ 12 = 3 layers. You're thinking in 3D!

questions.q: Solve for x: x + 7 = 15

questions.q: Solve for x: 3x = 21
questions.why: Undo the multiplication by dividing both sides by 3: x = 21 ÷ 3 = 7. You've got the balance scale idea!

questions.why: A variable like n is a placeholder for a number we don't know yet. It's a math detective's clue!

passages.title: The Line Around the Middle
passages.text: Cartographers draw an imaginary line around the widest part of the Earth and call it the equator. Because the planet is a sphere, that line splits it into a Northern Hemisphere and a Southern Hemisphere. Countries near the equator receive nearly the same amount of sunlight all year, so their seasons look nothing like ours. Sailors once used the line on their charts to keep track of latitude, and a navigator could tell how far north or south a ship had travelled by measuring the height of the sun at noon. The line is imaginary, but the differences it describes are real.

passages.title: One Fair Question
passages.text: A fair test begins with one question that can be answered with numbers. First you write a hypothesis, which is a prediction you could prove wrong. Then you list the steps, choose what you will change, and decide what you will measure. Only one thing changes in a fair test, because if two things change you can never tell which one caused the result. Observations go into the lab notebook as you work, with units beside every number. When the data is complete, you look for a pattern before you write the conclusion. A conclusion that ignores the data is only a story.

passages.title: Sailing by the Stars
passages.text: Long before satellites, navigators crossed oceans using a compass and a table of stars. Vasco da Gama rounded the tip of Africa and reached India by sea in 1498, following a route that European ships had never sailed. Twenty years later Magellan's expedition set out to circle the whole world, and one ship completed the journey. These voyages changed the maps that people kept at home, because lands that had been drawn as guesses became coastlines with names. Exploration also brought conquest and disease, which is why a modern history book tells the voyages from more than one side.

passages.title: Fractions at the Counter
passages.text: A recipe for granola calls for three quarters of a cup of oats and half a cup of nuts. If you double the recipe, you multiply every fraction by two: three quarters becomes six quarters, which is one whole cup and a half. Cooking is one of the few places where an improper fraction appears on a Tuesday morning, and nobody stops to worry about it. The denominator never changes its job, because it still tells you how many equal parts make a whole. Measure carefully, keep the units straight, and the batch will come out the same way twice.
